```{python}
# Headline corpus quantities used in the front matter, computed once from the
# analysis universe (S&P 500 at 2021-01-01; the DuckDB manifest views are

from pathlib import Path
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

_db = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not _db.exists():
    _db = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
_db = _db.resolve()  # absolute: the chunk chdir()s to the repo root below
PANEL_DOCS = ("accession_number IN ("
              "SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND accession_number IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT document_id FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND document_id IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')")
import os
_repo_root = _db.resolve().parent.parent
_cwd0 = os.getcwd()
os.chdir(_repo_root)  # gold_ai_frames view reads part files by repo-relative path
_c = duckdb.connect(str(_db), read_only=True)
hd_n_docs, hd_n_paragraphs = _c.execute(
    f"SELECT count(DISTINCT accession_number), count(*) FROM paragraphs WHERE country_code = 'us' "
    f"AND form IN ('10-K', '10-Q', '20-F', 'DEF 14A', '8-K', 'Earnings call') AND {PANEL_DOCS}").fetchone()
hd_n_universe = _c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us'").fetchone()[0]
_c.close()
os.chdir(_cwd0)
_ap = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not _ap.exists():
    _ap = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
_a = pd.read_parquet(_ap, columns=["ticker", "text_hash", "activity_index"]).drop_duplicates()

hd_paragraphs_m = f"{hd_n_paragraphs / 1e6:.1f}"

# Headline results quoted in the front matter and conclusions, read from the
# same artifacts the empirical chapters compute them from.
import json
_cl = _ap.parent
_m = pd.read_parquet(_cl / "firm_year_master_v2.parquet")
_yr = _m.groupby("year").agg(any_ai=("any_ai", "mean"), frames=("frames_per_1k", "mean"))
hd_share = {int(y): float(v * 100) for y, v in _yr["any_ai"].items()}
hd_frames = {int(y): float(v) for y, v in _yr["frames"].items()}
hd_frames_ratio = hd_frames[2025] / hd_frames[2021]
hd_frames_ratio_26 = hd_frames[2026] / hd_frames[2021]

# Same-window seasonal adjustment for the partial 2026 year: the change in a
# measure between the 2025 window that ends on the same calendar day as the
# 2026 cut-off and the full 2025 year is applied to the 2026 year-to-date value.
_dp = pd.read_parquet(_cl / "document_panel.parquet")
_dp = _dp[_dp["form"].isin(["10-K", "10-Q", "DEF 14A", "8-K"])].copy()
_dp["year"] = _dp["fecha"].dt.year
_dp["md"] = _dp["fecha"].dt.month * 100 + _dp["fecha"].dt.day
hd_cutoff = _dp.loc[_dp["year"] == 2026, "fecha"].max()
hd_cutoff_md = int(hd_cutoff.month * 100 + hd_cutoff.day)
hd_cutoff_str = hd_cutoff.strftime("%-d %B")

def _fy_measures(sub):
    g = sub.groupby("ticker").agg(w=("n_words", "sum"), fr=("n_frames", "sum"))
    return float((1000 * g["fr"] / g["w"]).mean()), float((g["fr"] > 0).mean() * 100)

_full25 = _fy_measures(_dp[_dp["year"] == 2025])
_win25 = _fy_measures(_dp[(_dp["year"] == 2025) & (_dp["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)])
_ytd26 = _fy_measures(_dp[(_dp["year"] == 2026) & (_dp["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)])
hd_int_factor = _full25[0] / _win25[0]
hd_share_factor = _full25[1] / _win25[1]
hd_int_est_2026 = _ytd26[0] * hd_int_factor
hd_share_est_2026 = min(_ytd26[1] * hd_share_factor, 100.0)
hd_int_ratio_est = hd_int_est_2026 / hd_frames[2021]
# Activity volumes: same-window factor on the activity count itself.
_ad = pd.read_parquet(_ap, columns=["accession_number", "text_hash", "activity_index"]).drop_duplicates()
_ad = _ad.merge(pd.read_parquet(_cl / "document_panel.parquet", columns=["accession_number", "fecha"]), on="accession_number", how="inner")
_ad["year"] = _ad["fecha"].dt.year
_ad["md"] = _ad["fecha"].dt.month * 100 + _ad["fecha"].dt.day
hd_act_factor = float(((_ad["year"] == 2025).sum()) / ((_ad["year"] == 2025) & (_ad["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)).sum())
os.chdir(_repo_root)
_c = duckdb.connect(str(_db), read_only=True)
_tenk = _c.execute(f"""
    SELECT extract(year FROM fm.filing_date)::INT AS y,
           count(DISTINCT p.accession_number) AS docs,
           count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN f.accession_number IS NOT NULL THEN p.accession_number END) AS docs_ai
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT accession_number FROM paragraphs WHERE country_code = 'us' AND form = '10-K' AND {PANEL_DOCS}) p
    JOIN filing_manifest fm ON fm.accession_number = p.accession_number AND fm.country_code = 'us'
    LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT accession_number FROM gold_ai_frames WHERE country_code = 'us' AND has_frame AND form = '10-K') f
           ON f.accession_number = p.accession_number
    GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
""").df()
_c.close()
os.chdir(_cwd0)
hd_tenk_share = {int(r.y): float(r.docs_ai / r.docs * 100) for r in _tenk.itertuples()}
_gapw = json.loads((_cl / "channel_gap_words_robustness.json").read_text())
hd_promo_ratio = _gapw["promo_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
hd_quant_ratio = _gapw["quant_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
_sm = json.loads((_cl / "strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())
hd_corr = _sm["correlation_matrix"]
hd_stab = {int(k): v for k, v in _sm["stability_by_k"].items()}
hd_stab3 = dict(zip(_sm["cluster_sizes"].keys(), hd_stab[3])) if len(_sm["cluster_sizes"]) == 3 else {}
hd_pca_ev = [x * 100 for x in _sm["pca_diagnostic"]["explained_variance_ratio"]]
_var = _sm["activity_volume_regression"]
hd_vs_ratio = _var["volume_adjusted"]["Vocal Substantives"]["ratio"]
hd_gl_ratio = _var["volume_adjusted"]["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["ratio"]
hd_vol_r2 = _var["r2_adjusted"]
_wv = json.loads((_cl / "washing_score_validation.json").read_text())
hd_w_rho = _wv["persistence"]["spearman"]
_apj = json.loads((_cl / "activity_profiles.json").read_text())
hd_quant_pooled = _apj["top_behaviours"]["quantified_outcome"]
hd_quant_filings = _apj["top_behaviours_filings_only"]["quantified_outcome"]
hd_obj_unspec_firms = _apj["object_families"]["AI, unspecified object"]["pct_firms"]
hd_src_unspec = _apj["distributions"]["ai_source"]["unspecified"]
_inc = json.loads((_cl / "incremental_signal.json").read_text())["outcomes"]["beta"]
hd_inc_n = int(_inc["n_washing"])
hd_inc_r2_base = _inc["r2_M2AB_washing_sample"]
hd_inc_r2_w = _inc["r2_M4"]
hd_inc_dr2 = _inc["delta_r2_washing"]
hd_inc_F = _inc["wald_washing"]["F"]
hd_inc_p = _inc["wald_washing"]["p"]
_cg = json.loads((_cl / "activity_grounding.json").read_text())["channel_gap"]["pooled"]
hd_gap_quant_pp = _cg["quantified_outcome"]["gap_pp"]
hd_gap_named_pp = _cg["named_product_or_process"]["gap_pp"]
```

# Executive Summary {.unnumbered}

Between 2021 and 2026 almost every S&P 500 firm started talking about AI, so counting mentions no longer tells us much. This thesis builds a scalable framework that separates how much firms talk about AI from what they claim to be doing. It also measures how concretely those AI activities are supported and whether the talk runs ahead of disclosed substance.

We use `{python} hd_paragraphs_m` million paragraphs from the SEC filings and earnings calls of the S&P 500 as constituted in January 2021. We add an inventory of `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` discrete AI activities disclosed by `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` of those firms. The main result is that corporate AI is mostly an application-layer story: firms describe putting AI into products, workflows, customer service, and internal operations, not building foundational technology. Still, firms follow three stable disclosure strategies. Vocal Substantives pair heavy communication with large, mature AI activity portfolios and are the only group with distinctive financial fundamentals. Governance-Led and Defensive Disclosers copy the oversight or risk language of their industries with far less disclosed activity behind it. The generative-AI boom multiplied disclosed activity several-fold without improving its grounding, and the external AI technology firms rely on is still heavily concentrated in U.S.-based providers.

Credibility is tested where disclosure becomes costly. Earnings calls carry about `{python} round(hd_promo_ratio)` times more promotional claims and `{python} round(hd_quant_ratio)` times more quantified claims per thousand words than statutory filings. Within the same firm and fiscal year, both venues describe the same activities. Yet the share backed by a quantified outcome is `{python} f"{hd_gap_quant_pp:.0f}"` percentage points lower in the filings. The story travels to the binding venue; much of the evidence does not.

Direct SEC scrutiny of AI claims has so far reached one firm in this universe. That firm answered with more AI text, not better-grounded AI text. In the market, the volume of a firm's AI rhetoric, not its disclosed substance, is what relates to later systematic risk. The gap between the two is not priced. None of this evidence is causal.

We turn these findings into an AI Disclosure Credibility Framework that combines Disclosure Intensity, Communication Posture, Disclosed AI Activity, AI Activity Grounding, Disclosed Substance, Decoupling, and cross-venue consistency. For issuers, the advice is simple: move evidence, not adjectives, into the 10-K. Name the action, the object, and the deployment stage, and carry the quantified outcomes from the call into the filing. For investors, the framework is a scalable way to decide how deep due diligence should go. A large gap between narrative and disclosed substance is a reason to read more closely, not a verdict.

# Introduction

## Business problem

After ChatGPT, almost every large company started talking about AI. Prior work documents the surge in annual-report AI language [@anantharaman2026, pp. 1--2]. The corpus built for this thesis shows the same pattern. The share of S&P 500 firms with any AI statement in their SEC filings rose from `{python} f"{hd_share[2021]:.0f}"`% in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.0f}"`% in 2025. It reaches an estimated `{python} f"{hd_share_est_2026:.0f}"`% at the close of 2026. Narrative intensity per thousand words grew an estimated `{python} f"{hd_int_ratio_est:.0f}"`-fold over the same period. Once nearly everyone talks about AI, mentioning it no longer separates real technological AI activity from strategic positioning.

This is a practical problem for three groups:

- **Investors** need to tell credible operational exposure from narrative positioning; studies of filings separate actionable or implemented AI from speculative claims and link that distinction to valuation [@basnet2025, pp. 1--2; @song2026, pp. 1--2].
- **Issuers** need to communicate material AI activity without creating expectations they cannot support, or legal exposure.
- **Regulators** are looking harder at whether public claims are backed up [@gensler2023, pp. 4--5; @sec2024pressrelease, pp. 1--2]. The SEC’s 2025 Welltower comment letter shows that inconsistencies across calls, press releases, and statutory filings can themselves draw regulatory attention [@welltower2025letter, p. 1].

Conventional mention counts [@loughran2011, p. 36] cannot solve this problem because they treat generic risk boilerplate and specific claims about deployed products, metrics, or providers the same way. So this thesis measures not only how much firms discuss AI, but what they claim and which AI activities they disclose. It also measures how concretely those AI activities are grounded and whether the claims hold up across disclosure venues.

## Research questions

The overarching question is: **can the content of corporate AI disclosure distinguish talk from disclosed substance, and does that distinction carry useful economic information?**

Four linked questions organize the empirical chapters:

- **RQ1: Evolution and composition.** How has corporate AI disclosure evolved, and what AI activities do firms report?
- **RQ2: Heterogeneity.** What recurrent disclosure profiles distinguish firms, and how do those profiles relate to firm economics?
- **RQ3: Credibility and decoupling.** Where do gaps emerge between disclosure and disclosed substance, and between statutory filings and earnings calls?
- **RQ4: Economic relevance.** Does AI disclosure carry economic information and relate to market outcomes?

## Literature on corporate AI disclosure and AI washing

### The emerging empirical frontier

The wave of commercial interest in artificial intelligence after ChatGPT produced a fast-growing empirical literature. It builds on textual-analysis traditions in finance and accounting [@li2008, pp. 1--3; @loughran2011, pp. 35--36; @gentzkow2019, pp. 1--2]. Recent studies examine corporate AI language in annual filings [@anantharaman2026, pp. 1--2] and distinguish actionable from speculative claims [@basnet2025, pp. 1--2]. Others separate planned from implemented AI using patents [@song2026, pp. 1--2], or build generative-AI exposure from occupational employment shares [@eisfeldt2023, p. 9].

At the same time, market participants and regulators have raised concerns about "AI washing": corporate AI claims with no observable implementation behind them [@gensler2023, pp. 4--5; @sec2024pressrelease, pp. 1--2]. This work borrows from the literature on greenwashing and symbolic management [@delmas2011, pp. 64--68; @lyon2015, pp. 1--3; @marquis2016, pp. 483--85]. It points to the same need: separating corporate rhetoric from grounded technological substance.

### Gaps in the literature and methodological responses

Despite rapid progress, existing research on corporate AI disclosure and AI washing has four limitations:

1. **Keyword retrieval treats mentions too coarsely.** Existing studies classify AI mentions as actionable or speculative [@anantharaman2026, pp. 1--2; @basnet2025, p. 1; @song2026, pp. 1--2], but keyword search cannot tell empty risk-factor boilerplate from specific, falsifiable claims. *This thesis extracts structured semantic frames (subject, tense, domain, promotional tone, sentence evidence) instead of relying on unparsed text.*
2. **No operational AI activity inventory.** Prior studies estimate aggregate firm-level exposure or mention counts [@song2026, pp. 1--2; @eisfeldt2023, p. 9], but do not record the concrete actions firms take. *This thesis builds an inventory of `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` discrete operational AI activity claims across `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` S&P 500 firms, classifying the action, object, business function, operational stage, sourcing, and evidence behind each claim.*
3. **Reliance on a single channel, the annual filing.** Prior AI studies focus almost only on Form 10-K filings. Earnings calls are a voluntary channel with different managerial incentives and less formality [@matsumoto2011, pp. 1383--84; @frankel1999, pp. 133--34]. *This thesis compares the same firm-years across statutory filings and earnings calls using firm $\times$ fiscal-year fixed effects to measure cross-venue credibility gaps.*
4. **No observable ground-truth census.** Environmental disclosures can be checked against audited emissions data [@delmas2011, pp. 68--69; @marquis2016, pp. 486--87]; firm-level AI deployment has no comparable external census. *The thesis therefore defines decoupling ($W$) strictly as the observable gap between a firm's narrative intensity and its own disclosed, grounded AI activity. It measures internal consistency, not unobservable fraud.*

## Theoretical foundations

Three conceptual traditions motivate the empirical designs:

- **Signalling and cheap talk.** A claim is more credible when it contains details that are costly to fake or easy to verify [@spence1973, pp. 363--64; @dye1985, pp. 123--24; @crawford1982, pp. 1431--32]. This is why we separate generic promotional language from named products, deployment stages, quantified metrics, and identifiable partners [@rogers2011, pp. 2155--56].
- **Institutional legitimacy.** Under technological uncertainty, organizations adopt fashionable language and symbols because stakeholders expect them, whether or not operations change [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41; @dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48; @suchman1995, pp. 571--74]. This is why we look at the market-wide diffusion and the cross-sectional clustering of AI disclosure postures.
- **Decoupling and symbolic management.** Organizational research separates formal structures from what the organization actually does day to day [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41; @westphal1994, pp. 367--69; @crilly2012, pp. 1429--31; @merkldavies2007, pp. 116--18]. Since actual corporate adoption has no audited census, this thesis measures observable decoupling between narrative volume and disclosed, grounded AI activity.

These foundations give us the measurement chain that organizes every empirical result: $\boxed{D \longrightarrow P \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow S \longrightarrow W}$, where $D$ is Disclosure Intensity (how much a firm talks about AI). $P$ is Communication Posture (how it talks), $A$ is Disclosed AI Activity (what it says it does), and $G$ is AI Activity Grounding (how concretely each activity is supported). $S$ is Disclosed Substance (activity volume weighted by grounding), and $W$ is Decoupling (the gap between the rank of $D$ and the rank of $S$).

The three theories give four testable hypotheses, one per research question:

- **H1 (RQ1, institutional legitimacy).** AI language spreads as an institutional norm, not as a report of new capability: diffusion is fast and near-universal, and after the generative-AI shock disclosed activity volume grows faster than its grounding.
- **H2 (RQ2, legitimacy and signalling).** Disclosure postures cluster by industry norm, but only the posture that pairs promotion with costly-to-fabricate detail is associated with distinct firm fundamentals.
- **H3 (RQ3, cheap talk).** Because earnings calls carry less liability, the same firm-year places more promotional and more quantified claims in calls than in statutory filings. It does so while describing the same mix of activities. Where direct regulatory scrutiny of AI claims occurs, what follows is more AI disclosure, not measurably better-grounded AI disclosure.
- **H4 (RQ4, signalling).** Markets read content, not volume: grounded activity carries information about later systematic risk beyond disclosure volume, and decoupling adds little once both are observed. The cheap-talk alternative is that only volume matters.

## Contribution

This thesis makes three contributions. First, a scalable measurement architecture that separates AI disclosure volume, communication posture, disclosed AI activity, grounding, and decoupling across `{python} f"{hd_n_docs:,}"` corporate filings and earnings calls. Second, it puts within-disclosure, cross-venue, regulatory, and market evidence side by side instead of treating AI disclosure as a mention-count problem. Third, it turns these measurements into a practical credibility framework for issuer communication and investor due diligence. @tbl-theory-to-test maps the theoretical foundations, research questions, and empirical tests to the chapters that follow.

# Methodology

## Data sources and corpus

The U.S. corpus covers 10-K, 10-Q, 20-F, DEF 14A, and 8-K filings for the S&P 500 universe plus earnings-call transcripts, from 2021 through a partial 2026. Document counts and deduplication totals are computed from the current processed corpus when the document is rendered. This U.S. corpus carries the embeddings, prefilter scores, and semantic frames, and every result in this thesis rests on it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

db_path = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not db_path.exists():
    db_path = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
_u = con.execute("SELECT active_status, count(*) AS n FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us' GROUP BY 1").df()
con.close()
uni_frame_total = int(_u["n"].sum())
uni_frame_delisted = int(_u.loc[_u["active_status"] == "delisted", "n"].sum())

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_master = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_master_v2.parquet"))
uni_n_firms = int(_master["ticker"].nunique())
_yrs = _master.groupby("ticker")["year"].nunique()
bal_n = int((_yrs == 6).sum())
bal_share = (_master[_master["ticker"].isin(_yrs[_yrs == 6].index)]
             .groupby("year").apply(lambda s: (s["n_frames"] > 0).mean() * 100)).to_dict()
uni_n_activity_firms = int(pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))["ticker"].nunique())

# Temporal coverage of the partial 2026 year, from the manifests.
con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
_cov = con.execute("""
    SELECT form_type, count(DISTINCT ticker) AS firms, max(filing_date) AS last_date
    FROM (SELECT form_type, ticker, filing_date FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us'
          UNION ALL SELECT '10-Q', ticker, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')
    WHERE extract(year FROM filing_date) = 2026 GROUP BY 1
""").df().set_index("form_type")
_cov25 = con.execute("SELECT count(DISTINCT ticker) FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND form_type = '10-K' AND extract(year FROM filing_date) = 2025").fetchone()[0]
con.close()
cov_last_date = str(pd.to_datetime(_cov["last_date"].max()).date())
cov_10k_2026 = int(_cov.loc["10-K", "firms"]) if "10-K" in _cov.index else 0
cov_10k_2025 = int(_cov25)
cov_10q_2026 = int(_cov.loc["10-Q", "firms"]) if "10-Q" in _cov.index else 0
cov_calls_2026 = int(_cov.loc["Earnings call transcript", "firms"]) if "Earnings call transcript" in _cov.index else 0
cov_months_2026 = pd.to_datetime(cov_last_date).month
```

**Firm universe.** We take the S&P 500 as it stood on 2021-01-01: `{python} uni_frame_total` tickers. `{python} uni_frame_delisted` of them were later delisted or acquired; we keep them, with their filings up to the exit date, so the sample does not suffer from survivorship bias. Firms that joined the index after that date are excluded. `{python} uni_n_firms` of the `{python} uni_frame_total` firms have at least one processed document, and `{python} uni_n_activity_firms` disclose at least one operational AI activity. Finally, `{python} bal_n` firms appear in every year from 2021 to 2026; these form the balanced cohort used for diffusion checks. Some tables and regressions use a narrower sample: firms with call transcripts, or firms with enough AI text in both venues. Others use the firm-years of a single fiscal year. In those cases the sample size appears next to the estimate.

**Temporal coverage.** The panel closes with documents available on `{python} cov_last_date`, so 2026 is a partial year. `{python} cov_10k_2026` firms have filed a 2026 annual report (against `{python} cov_10k_2025` in 2025); 10-Qs cover two quarters (`{python} cov_10q_2026` firms) and call transcripts three (`{python} cov_calls_2026` firms). Two conventions follow. Non-accumulating measures (archetype assignments, Decoupling, grounding shares, the 2026 reporting-season screen) are reported as observed year to date. Measures compared across years (share of firms disclosing AI, frames per thousand words, activity counts) are given as observed and as a full-year 2026 estimate. The estimate uses a same-window seasonal adjustment. It scales the 2026 year-to-date value by the ratio of full-year 2025 to the 2025 window ending on the 2026 cut-off day (`{python} hd_cutoff_str`). This corrects for the seasonal document mix rather than assuming an even filing calendar. Figures flag estimates as projections; 2025 remains the last complete year.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path
import duckdb
from IPython.display import Markdown

db_path = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not db_path.exists():
    db_path = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
# Documents of the analysis universe (S&P 500 at 2021-01-01). The manifest
# views are already restricted to that panel; `paragraphs` is a base table
# keyed by accession_number (calls use their document_id), so every corpus
# count joins back to the manifests through this predicate.
PANEL_DOCS = ("accession_number IN ("
              "SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND accession_number IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT document_id FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND document_id IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')")
scope = f"country_code = 'us' AND form IN ('10-K', '10-Q', '20-F', 'DEF 14A', '8-K', 'Earnings call') AND {PANEL_DOCS}"
totals = con.execute(f"""
    SELECT count(DISTINCT accession_number) AS documents,
           count(*) AS paragraphs,
           sum(is_scorable::INT) AS scorable,
           count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN is_scorable THEN text_hash END) AS unique_texts
    FROM paragraphs WHERE {scope}
""").fetchone()
con.close()
Markdown(
    f"The current processed corpus contains **{totals[0]:,} documents** and "
    f"**{totals[1]:,} paragraph instances**. The length-and-content filter retains "
    f"{totals[2]:,} scorable instances, which deduplicate to {totals[3]:,} unique texts."
)
```

*Notes: High-level overview of the six-stage inference funnel. Granular form-by-form decompositions (10-K, 10-Q, DEF 14A, 8-K, Earnings Calls, and 20-F) and intermediate model acceptance diagnostics are reported in @tbl-a1-funnel-full (Appendix A).*

The pipeline turns raw corporate text into two structured layers: semantic claims, which capture how firms talk about AI, and disclosed AI activities, which capture what firms say they are doing. These two layers are then aggregated into the measurement constructs used throughout the thesis:

$$\text{Raw text} \longrightarrow \text{AI claims} \longrightarrow \text{Disclosed AI activities} \longrightarrow \text{Firm-level measures}$$

The architecture follows the standard KDD/CRISP-DM sequence: data selection and preprocessing, then inference, validation, and analysis [@fayyad1996, pp. 40--41; @shearer2000, pp. 15--19].

## Identifying AI disclosure: cleaning, deduplication, and ML gate

Before any language model reads a paragraph, the text stack cleans, deduplicates, and filters it. Each scorable paragraph is hashed on its normalized text (BLAKE2b), which collapses `{python} f"{totals[2] / 1e6:.2f}"` million scorable paragraph instances into `{python} f"{totals[3] / 1e6:.2f}"` million unique texts. Everything downstream runs once per unique hash, not once per document, and the results are joined back to every filing that contains that text. This keeps the computation manageable and stops recycled boilerplate and legal disclaimers from being scored again and again.

The prefilter is a supervised gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT). It scores 39 lexical, semantic, structural, and sentence-level signals in four groups. The first is keywords and named entities. The second is cosine similarity between the paragraph's sentence embedding (a numeric vector that summarizes its meaning) and a set of reference AI concepts. The third and fourth are document geometry and syntactic cues. We tuned the classifier for high recall ($\ge 0.92$ across all document types) on purpose. A false positive is cheap because the LLM pass rejects it later, but a missed mention is gone for good. Held-out performance and inter-judge evaluations are reported in @tbl-evaluation-datasets.

In total, the gate flags `{python} f"{n_prefiltered:,}"` candidate unique texts: `{python} f"{n_prefiltered / n_unique * 100:.1f}"`% of the unique texts and `{python} f"{n_prefiltered / n_scorable * 100:.1f}"`% of scorable paragraph instances. Documents with no AI disclosure are recorded as true zeros, not as missing values.

## From paragraphs to individual AI claims: frame extraction

Every text the prefilter flags goes to a zero-shot large language model (LLM) judge, Qwen 3.7 Flash, the same model used for every extraction step in this thesis. The judge separates real corporate AI discourse from stray keywords, boilerplate disclaimers, and macroeconomic commentary, and extracts zero, one, or several structured claims ("frames") per text. Instead of reading a disclosure as one undifferentiated narrative, it breaks each claim into a standard eight-dimension schema (@tbl-frame-schema).

This pass is a high-precision gate: `{python} f"{(1 - n_framed / n_prefiltered) * 100:.1f}"`% of the prefilter candidates contain no real AI claim and are dropped. In total, `{python} f"{n_prefiltered:,}"` candidate texts yield `{python} f"{n_frames_total:,}"` validated semantic frames, and `{python} f"{share_firm_subject:.1f}"`% of those describe actions or exposures of the disclosing firm itself. These frames are the raw material for AI Disclosure Intensity ($D$) and Communication Posture ($P$).

## From claims to a list of concrete AI activities: action, object, and function

When a frame describes the disclosing firm doing something operational with AI (deploying, developing, partnering, investing, hiring, or scaling), it goes into a second extraction prompt. This pass runs only on the `{python} f"{n_firm_texts:,}"` unique texts whose frames have the disclosing firm as subject. It solves an attribution problem. The prompt receives the firm's identity (ticker and legal name), so the model can tell a proprietary internal tool apart from a vendor integration, a co-development, or a client implementation.

For each operational claim, the model extracts an action triple (action, object, function): what the firm does, to what, and in which business function. It also extracts maturity stage, technology sourcing, target beneficiaries, named commercial entities, and evidence flags (@tbl-activity-schema). Every record is anchored to the exact sentence indices in the source filing. Across the corpus, this pass recovers `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` unique operational AI activity claims from `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` S&P 500 firms. These are the raw material for Disclosed AI Activity ($A$) and AI Activity Grounding ($G$).

## From extracted evidence to analytical constructs

The two extracted layers, semantic frames and disclosed AI activities, combine into the six constructs used throughout the empirical analysis:

$$\underbrace{\text{Semantic frames}}_{\text{frame extraction}} \Longrightarrow D, P$$

$$\underbrace{\text{AI Activity records}}_{\text{activity extraction}} \Longrightarrow A, G$$

$$(D, A, G) \Longrightarrow S \Longrightarrow W$$

1. **AI Disclosure Intensity ($D$):** How much a firm talks about AI, measured as AI semantic claims per 1,000 words of scorable narrative text:
   $$D_{it} = \frac{\text{AI frames}_{it}}{\text{words}_{it} / 1{,}000}$$
   Every intensity figure in this thesis uses words as the denominator, so documents of different lengths sit on the same scale.
2. **Communication Posture ($P$):** How a firm talks about AI, captured on six standard dimensions: claim realization, risk orientation, governance orientation, claim specificity, customer-facing orientation, and promotional tone.
3. **Disclosed AI Activity ($A$):** Discrete operational claims ($n_{\text{activities}}$) from the firm-conditioned LLM pass, covering concrete actions across six business domains.
4. **AI Activity Grounding ($G$):** An unweighted verifiability index in $[0, 1]$, equal to the share of five checks that a firm's disclosed AI activities pass. The checks are a specific business function, a deployed or scaled stage, a named product or process, a quantified metric, and a named technology provider.
5. **Disclosed Substance ($S$):** Grounded operational AI activity volume, which grows with the log of the activity count and linearly with grounding quality:
   $$S_{it} = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities},it}) \times G_{it}$$
6. **Decoupling ($W$):** The signed percentile-rank gap between narrative volume and grounded substance, with ranks computed over all disclosing firm-years in the panel. Persistent positive decoupling is what this thesis means by the colloquial term "AI washing"; the construct is always called Decoupling and always written $W$:
   $$W_{it} = \text{rank}(D_{it}) - \text{rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]$$

Different questions call for different units of observation:

- the **unique text** (deduplicated paragraph, unit of prefiltering and frame scoring);
- the **semantic frame** (individual claim about AI);
- the **disclosed AI activity** (action-object-function operational triple);
- the **document** (unit of narrative intensity, joining frames back to document instances);
- the **pooled firm** (unit of the communication posture archetypes);
- the **firm-year** (unit of Decoupling $W$ and of the fundamentals regressions);
- the **firm $\times$ fiscal-year $\times$ venue cell** (unit of the cross-venue comparisons);
- the **firm-date event** (unit of the earnings-call market regressions); and
- the **treated firm and its matched peers** (unit of the SEC comment-letter case comparison).

To go from documents to firm-years, we combine document intensity rates with the median rather than a length-weighted mean. A single long exhibit or a boilerplate risk section therefore cannot pull the annual score. In practice, 10-Q filings rarely carry much AI narrative, so the 10-K dominates the annual figure and the median and the weighted average agree to several decimal places across the panel.

For operational concepts (deployments, governance, risks), we use log-transformed counts rather than shares of total AI discourse, because counts are far more stable on test-retest ($\rho = 0.845$ for counts vs. $0.528$ for shares). Finally, firm-level rates for firms with little AI text are shrunk empirically toward the corpus mean, so that a handful of paragraphs cannot inflate the variance of sparse disclosers.

## Financial and market variables

Firm-year financial and market variables come from XBRL and price data. They are aligned on the actual fiscal period end rather than the filing date. Concept coverage relies on documented fallback chains (capex 91%, SG&A 81%, net margin 99%, revenue 99%) and a [340, 380]-day gap rule to validate year-over-year changes. The variable set used throughout the empirical analysis is market capitalization, R&D-to-sales, gross margin, operating margin, asset turnover, price-to-sales, next-fiscal-year revenue growth, market beta, and idiosyncratic volatility. Idiosyncratic volatility is the annualized standard deviation of one-factor market-model residuals over the 252 trading days before the filing.

R&D-to-sales has only 46% XBRL coverage, so we use it as an outcome and not as a general control. It picks out firms that separately report comparable current R&D instead of treating non-reporting as zero. Appendix D gives the beta specification, its estimation-window diagnostics, the treatment of delisted firms, and the R&D coverage assessment. All financial ratios are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

## Measurement validation: golden sets and model benchmarks

Every automated stage of the pipeline is checked against held-out ground truth, a second model acting as an independent judge, and manual human audits. The evaluation datasets, how each sample was built, and the performance metrics are listed in @tbl-evaluation-datasets.

| Benchmark dataset | What it validates | Forms | Sample size | Labels from | Metric / performance |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| **LLM-labeled reference set (prefilter training and test)** | Machine-learning gate: does a paragraph discuss AI? | 10-K, 10-Q | 9,900 texts | Qwen 3.7 Flash, cross-checked by Gemini 3.8 | F1 = 0.96 (Prec. 0.98, Rec. 0.94) on held-out texts |
| **Inter-judge agreement** | Frame classification: do two independent models assign the same frame dimensions? | 10-K, 10-Q | 6,038 pairs | Gemini 3.8 vs. Qwen 3.7 Flash | Cohen's $\kappa = 0.81–0.87$ across dimensions (agreement beyond chance; 1 = perfect) |
| **Out-of-domain proxy statements and 8-Ks** | Gate transfer to forms not used in training | DEF 14A, 8-K | 1,500 texts | Qwen 3.7 Flash | Prec. 0.73, Rec. 0.92; F1 = 0.82 (14A), 0.65 (8-K) |
| **Out-of-domain earnings calls** | Gate transfer to transcripts | Transcripts | 800 texts | Qwen 3.7 Flash | Prec. 0.59, Rec. 0.98, F1 = 0.73 (Prec. 0.85 on strong positives) |
| **Semantic anchors** | Gate inputs: reference sentences describing AI concepts against which paragraph similarity is scored | All forms | 27 anchors | Expert curated | 39 gate signals, including similarity to the anchors |
| **Activity extraction audit** | Activity fields (function, stage, entity role) that feed $A$, $G$, $S$ and $W$ | Mixed sample | 120 paragraphs, 267 activities | Human audit (purpose-built annotation interface) | Field agreement 92.4% (function), 89.1% (stage), 95.8% (entity role) |
| **Human ground truth (frames)** | Frame extraction against human coders | All forms | 720 texts | Human coders (purpose-built annotation interface) | Agreement 89.1%–95.8% across fields; Prec. 91.2%, Rec. 88.7% |
| **External benchmark: AI patents** | Whether $A$, $G$ and $W$ order firms like an independent, non-textual measure of AI capacity | 10-K, 10-Q, DEF 14A, 8-K, calls | Universe firms with matched patents, 2021–2024 | Google Patents / OECD 2025 AI taxonomy | Spearman ρ ≈ 0.5 between disclosed (and grounded) activity and AI patents; archetypes sort in the predicted order (Appendix B) |

: Labeled evaluation datasets, validation benchmarks, and inter-judge agreement. {#tbl-evaluation-datasets}

*Notes:* All operational labels used in the empirical chapters come from zero-shot LLM extraction. The reference set used to train the gate is itself LLM-labeled, so it is a consistency benchmark rather than human ground truth. Human ground truth enters through the 720-text frame audit and the 267-activity field audit. The inter-judge agreement ($\kappa = 0.81–0.87$) and the human audits show that the results hold across two different foundation model families (Google Gemini vs. Alibaba Qwen) and against human coders.

# Corporate AI Disclosure Strategies

## AI becomes ubiquitous

AI went from a niche topic to a standard item of corporate disclosure between 2021 and 2026. The share of S&P 500 firms making at least one AI statement in their SEC filings rose from `{python} f"{hd_share[2021]:.1f}"`% in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.1f}"`% in 2025, the last complete year. It reached `{python} f"{hd_share[2026]:.1f}"`% in the 2026 year-to-date sample (@fig-ai-diffusion). Narrative intensity, AI semantic frames per 1,000 words of corporate text, climbed from `{python} f"{hd_frames[2021]:.3f}"` in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_frames[2025]:.3f}"` in 2025 (`{python} f"{hd_frames_ratio:.1f}"`-fold). It stands at `{python} f"{hd_frames[2026]:.3f}"` in 2026 year to date.

Year-to-date values are not comparable with full years because the document mix is seasonal: annual reports cluster in the first quarter. We therefore estimate full-year 2026 with a same-window adjustment. In 2025, the change from the window ending on `{python} hd_cutoff_str` to the full year was a factor of `{python} f"{hd_int_factor:.3f}"` for intensity and `{python} f"{hd_share_factor:.3f}"` for participation. Applied to the 2026 year-to-date values, those factors give an estimated `{python} f"{hd_int_est_2026:.3f}"` frames per 1,000 words (`{python} f"{hd_int_ratio_est:.1f}"`-fold since 2021) and `{python} f"{hd_share_est_2026:.1f}"`% participation at the close of 2026.

The sharpest jump comes in the 2023–2024 filing season, when fiscal-year-2023 10-Ks became the first annual reports written after a full year of generative AI commercialization. The share of 10-Ks with any AI content went from `{python} f"{hd_tenk_share[2023]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{hd_tenk_share[2024]:.0f}"`% in one season. A balanced cohort of the `{python} bal_n` firms observed every year from 2021 to 2026 follows the same path (`{python} f"{bal_share[2021]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{bal_share[2025]:.0f}"`%). This is market-wide adoption, not survivorship or index rebalancing.

Once almost every large firm talks about AI, presence alone says little. At `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.1f}"`% participation, *whether* a firm discloses AI no longer separates firms. What separates them is *how* they communicate: the framing, emphasis, risk perception, and specificity that make up their disclosure posture.

## The dimensions of AI disclosure strategy

Six frame-level dimensions describe Communication Posture ($P$); disclosure intensity $D$ completes the set. @tbl-strategy-dimensions defines each one and its managerial meaning; @fig-strategy-dimensions-dist shows their distribution across the S&P 500.

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the seven AI disclosure posture dimensions across the S&P 500 (white circle = median; blue bar = interquartile range; grey whisker = 5th–95th percentile)."

df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))

```

| Dimension | Operational Definition | Range | Managerial Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Promotional posture** | Average of promotional tone and strategic-importance framing | $[0, 1]$ | Extent to which AI is communicated as a transformative strategic asset |
| **Risk orientation** | Share of statements containing risk, uncertainty, or dependency concepts | $[0, 1]$ | Degree to which AI is treated as an operational vulnerability or hazard |
| **Governance orientation** | Share of statements containing oversight, ethics, or compliance policies | $[0, 1]$ | Formal institutionalization of model oversight and responsible AI guardrails |
| **Temporal posture** | Share of statements describing realized rather than planned actions | $[0, 1]$ | Operational maturity: active deployment vs. speculative roadmap |
| **AI positioning** | Share of statements framed toward clients and external products | $[0, 1]$ | Commercial orientation: revenue generation vs. internal cost-cutting |
| **Specificity** | Mean of 5 binary grounding flags (process, product, vendor, metric, timeline) | $[0, 1]$ | Falsifiability and informational granularity of corporate statements |
| **Disclosure intensity** | Percentile rank of AI semantic frames per 1,000 narrative words | $[0, 1]$ | Overall volume of narrative communication dedicated to artificial intelligence |

: Operational definitions of the seven AI disclosure strategy dimensions. {#tbl-strategy-dimensions}

The correlation structure of these seven dimensions shows two properties of corporate communication (full matrix in @tbl-a3-posture-correlation, Appendix C):

1. Governance framing is largely independent of the other dimensions. Governance orientation barely correlates with promotional posture ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['promotional_posture']:.2f}"`), risk framing ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['risk_orientation']:.2f}"`), or disclosure intensity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['disclosure_intensity']:.2f}"`). Governance disclosure is its own layer, not a proxy for verbosity or risk aversion.
2. Risk orientation runs against concrete execution. Risk framing correlates negatively with realized temporal posture ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['temporal_posture']:.2f}"`), specificity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['specificity']:.2f}"`), customer-facing positioning ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['ai_positioning']:.2f}"`), and intensity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['disclosure_intensity']:.2f}"`). Firms that treat AI mainly as a hazard say less about it, name fewer concrete artifacts, and rarely report client-facing deployments.

## Recurrent disclosure archetypes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_arch = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
arch_n_universe = len(_arch)
arch_n_noai = int((_arch["archetype"] == "No AI").sum())
arch_n_fit = arch_n_universe - arch_n_noai
```

We compute the posture dimensions for every firm in the `{python} arch_n_universe`-firm sampling universe. Firms with fewer than five AI frames across their pooled 2021–2025 SEC filings receive the rule-based label **No AI** ($n =$ `{python} arch_n_noai`). This way, firms that barely mention the technology are not given an artificial posture. As the institutional-legitimacy view predicts, firms adopt the language stakeholders expect [@dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48]. The residual group is small: by 2025 almost nine in ten index members have enough AI text to receive a posture.

For the remaining firms ($n =$ `{python} arch_n_fit`), we apply K-means clustering to the seven standardized posture dimensions. Three distinct, interpretable archetypes emerge (@fig-archetype-heatmap):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Disclosure archetypes at a glance: standardized (z-score) mean posture profile of the three K-means archetypes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))

FEATURES = ["promotional_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation",
           "temporal_posture", "ai_positioning", "specificity", "disclosure_intensity"]
LABELS = ["Promotional", "Risk", "Governance", "Temporal\n(realized)", "Customer-\nfacing", "Specificity", "Intensity"]
ARCHETYPES = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]

fit_pop = df[df["archetype"] != "No AI"]
z = (fit_pop[FEATURES] - fit_pop[FEATURES].mean()) / fit_pop[FEATURES].std(ddof=0)
z["archetype"] = fit_pop["archetype"].values
mat = z.groupby("archetype")[FEATURES].mean().reindex(ARCHETYPES)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 4.2), dpi=300)

```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-archetypes-glance
#| tbl-cap: "AI corporate disclosure archetypes at a glance. Posture profile reports the mean standardized score (SD from the pooled mean of clustered firms) on the dimensions that most separate each archetype; stability is the mean bootstrap Jaccard similarity of each firm's assignment."
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_g = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
_feats = {"promotional_posture": "promotional", "risk_orientation": "risk", "governance_orientation": "governance",
          "temporal_posture": "realized", "ai_positioning": "customer-facing", "specificity": "specificity",
          "disclosure_intensity": "intensity"}
_fit = _g[_g["archetype"] != "No AI"]
_z = (_fit[list(_feats)] - _fit[list(_feats)].mean()) / _fit[list(_feats)].std()
_z["archetype"] = _fit["archetype"].values
_zm = _z.groupby("archetype").mean()
_n = _g["archetype"].value_counts()
_stab = _g.groupby("archetype")["archetype_stability"].mean()
arch_share = (_n / len(_g) * 100).round(1).to_dict()

def _profile(a):
    row = _zm.loc[a].sort_values()
    hi = [f"{_feats[k]} (+{v:.2f} SD)" for k, v in row[row > 0.4].sort_values(ascending=False).items()]
    lo = [f"{_feats[k]} ({v:.2f} SD)" for k, v in row[row < -0.4].items()]
    parts = []
    if hi: parts.append("High " + ", ".join(hi))
    if lo: parts.append("low " + ", ".join(lo))
    return "; ".join(parts)

_rows = []
for a in ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]:
    _rows.append([f"**{a}**", int(_n[a]), f"{arch_share[a]:.1f}%", _profile(a), f"{_stab[a]:.2f}"])
_rows.append(["**No AI**", int(_n["No AI"]), f"{arch_share['No AI']:.1f}%",
              "Fewer than 5 pooled AI frames across 2021–2025 SEC filings (rule-based filter)", "1.00"])
Markdown(tabulate(_rows, headers=["Archetype", "Firms ($n$)", "Share (%)", "Posture profile", "Stability"]))
```

The three archetypes reflect different strategic orientations (@tbl-archetypes-glance). *Vocal Substantives* pair commercial promotion with high specificity and deployed applications. *Governance-Led Disclosers* stress oversight structures and model-risk controls and keep promotional claims measured. *Defensive Disclosers*, the largest group (`{python} f"{arch_share['Defensive Disclosers']:.1f}"`%), stick almost entirely to mandatory risk warnings with little operational detail. Through the signalling lens [@spence1973, pp. 363--64], only the first archetype consistently backs promotional language with detail that is costly to fake (named products, deployment stages, customer-facing use). That is what makes a claim informative. The other two differ mainly in the mandatory register they adopt, governance or risk.

## Are the archetypes real and stable

To check that the three clusters are real structure and not a partition forced by the algorithm, we test their stability with a non-parametric bootstrap. For each firm, we resample its own AI frames with replacement 25 times and rerun the full pipeline (posture dimensions, then K-means). We then compute the mean Jaccard similarity between the resampled clusters and the original assignments.

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-stability
#| fig-cap: "Choosing k by bootstrap stability: cluster stability evaluation across candidate values of k (25 resamples of each firm's own frames). Only k = 3 keeps every cluster above the 0.60 Jaccard floor."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

manifest = json.loads(_p("strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())
stab = manifest["stability_by_k"]
ks = [int(k) for k in stab.keys()]
means = [np.mean(stab[str(k)]) for k in ks]
mins = [np.min(stab[str(k)]) for k in ks]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.5), dpi=300)
for k in ks:
    scores = stab[str(k)]
    ax.scatter([k]*len(scores), scores, color="#3B82F6", alpha=0.65, s=45, zorder=3)

ax.plot(ks, means, "o-", color="#1D4ED8", lw=2.2, label="Mean Jaccard overlap", zorder=4)
ax.plot(ks, mins, "s--", color="#DC2626", lw=1.8, label="Minimum cluster Jaccard", zorder=4)
ax.axhline(0.60, color="#991B1B", linestyle=":", lw=1.4, label="Stability floor (0.60)", zorder=2)

for k, mn in zip(ks, mins):
    ax.annotate(f"{mn:.2f}", (k, mn), xytext=(0, -14), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold", color="#991B1B" if mn < 0.60 else "#0F172A")

ax.set_xticks(ks)
ax.set_xlabel("Number of Clusters (k)", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Bootstrap Jaccard Overlap", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylim(0.3, 1.0)
ax.set_title("Cluster Stability Evaluation Across Candidate Values of k (25 Resamples)", fontsize=10.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8.0, framealpha=0.9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

$k = 3$ is the largest number of clusters at which every cluster clears the 0.60 mean-Jaccard stability floor (@fig-archetype-stability; worst-recovered cluster at $k = 3$: `{python} f"{min(hd_stab[3]):.2f}"`; best: `{python} f"{max(hd_stab[3]):.2f}"`). At $k = 4$ the worst drops to `{python} f"{min(hd_stab[4]):.2f}"`, and at $k = 5$ to `{python} f"{min(hd_stab[5]):.2f}"`. So $k = 3$ (four groups once the deterministic No AI category is added) is the finest partition that still replicates.

A principal components analysis on the seven standardized dimensions confirms that the space cannot be collapsed into one score without heavy information loss. The first two components explain `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0] + hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`% of the variance (PC1: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0]:.1f}"`%, PC2: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`%) and PC3 adds another `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[2]:.1f}"`% (full diagnostic in @tbl-a3-pca-diagnostic, Appendix C). With variance spread over several orthogonal factors, the seven interpretable dimensions give managers clearer guidance than abstract latent factors would.

### Out-of-sample temporal validation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Out-of-sample temporal validation on firm-year posture vectors: fit k-means
# (k = 3) on the training window, assign 2025 firm-years to the frozen
# centroids, and compare with an unconstrained k-means refit on 2025 alone.
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_fy = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
_FE = ["promotional_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation", "temporal_posture",
       "ai_positioning", "specificity", "disclosure_intensity"]
_fy = _fy[(_fy["archetype"] != "No AI") & _fy[_FE].notna().all(axis=1)]

def _kmeans(X, k=3, seed=42, n_init=10, iters=300):
    best = None
    for s in range(n_init):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + s)
        C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]
        for _ in range(iters):
            lab = np.argmin(((X[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
            C2 = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(0) if (lab == j).any() else C[j] for j in range(k)])
            if np.allclose(C, C2):
                break
            C = C2
        inertia = ((X - C[lab]) ** 2).sum()
        if best is None or inertia < best[0]:
            best = (inertia, C, lab)
    return best[1], best[2]

def _ari(a, b):
    ct = pd.crosstab(a, b).values
    comb = lambda x: x * (x - 1) / 2
    n = ct.sum(); sij = comb(ct).sum(); si = comb(ct.sum(1)).sum(); sj = comb(ct.sum(0)).sum()
    e = si * sj / comb(n)
    return (sij - e) / ((si + sj) / 2 - e)

def _oos(train_years, test_year=2025):
    tr = _fy[_fy["year"].isin(train_years)]
    te = _fy[_fy["year"] == test_year]
    mu, sd = tr[_FE].mean(), tr[_FE].std()
    Xtr = ((tr[_FE] - mu) / sd).values
    Xte = ((te[_FE] - mu) / sd).values
    C, _ = _kmeans(Xtr)
    frozen = np.argmin(((Xte[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
    _, refit = _kmeans(Xte)
    # name frozen clusters by nearest pooled archetype centroid (label of the training rows)
    lab_tr = np.argmin(((Xtr[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
    names = {}
    for j in range(3):
        names[j] = tr["archetype"].values[lab_tr == j].tolist()
        names[j] = max(set(names[j]), key=names[j].count) if names[j] else f"cluster {j}"
    # per-archetype Jaccard recovery: best-matching refit cluster for each frozen cluster
    jac = {}
    for j in range(3):
        a = frozen == j
        jac[names[j]] = max(((a & (refit == r)).sum() / max((a | (refit == r)).sum(), 1)) for r in range(3)) * 100
    return _ari(frozen, refit), jac, len(te)

oos_ari_2124, oos_jac_2124, oos_n_2025 = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023, 2024])
oos_ari_2123, oos_jac_2123, _ = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023])
oos_ari_2125, _, oos_n_2026 = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025], test_year=2026)
oos_jac_min, oos_jac_max = min(oos_jac_2124.values()), max(oos_jac_2124.values())
oos_vs_2123 = oos_jac_2123.get("Vocal Substantives", float("nan"))
```

The taxonomy also holds out of sample. A model frozen on the 2021–2024 firm-years is applied to the `{python} oos_n_2025` firm-years of 2025. It reaches ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2124:.3f}"` (Adjusted Rand Index) against an unconstrained 2025 refit, with Jaccard recovery of `{python} f"{oos_jac_min:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{oos_jac_max:.1f}"`% across archetypes. Even the stricter pre-GenAI 2021–2023 training window keeps meaningful post-2023 recovery (ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2123:.3f}"`; Vocal Substantives recovered at `{python} f"{oos_vs_2123:.1f}"`%). The taxonomy is therefore not an artifact of the first commercialization wave. Freezing on 2021–2025 and testing on the `{python} oos_n_2026` firm-years observed so far in 2026 gives ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2125:.3f}"`. Posture rates do not depend on how much of the year has elapsed, so the partial year is a valid test set.

## Sectoral sorting of disclosure archetypes

Industry economics and regulatory exposure shape the archetypes strongly, though peers in the same sector still diverge. Comparing each sector's share of an archetype with its sample baseline shows clear sorting across the S&P 500 (@fig-sector-archetype-heatmap):

```{python}
#| label: fig-sector-archetype-heatmap

from pathlib import Path

db_path = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not db_path.exists():

con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
fu = con.execute("SELECT ticker, company_name, sic, active_status FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us'").df()
con.close()

def map_sector(sic2):
    try: s = int(sic2)
    except: return "Other"
    if s in [73, 35, 36]: return "Technology"
    elif s in [48]: return "Communications"
    elif s in [28, 38, 80]: return "Healthcare & Pharma"
    elif 60 <= s <= 67: return "Financial Services"
    elif 20 <= s <= 39: return "Industrials & Mfg"
    elif 40 <= s <= 47: return "Transportation"
    elif s == 49: return "Utilities"
    elif 10 <= s <= 14 or s == 29: return "Energy & Mining"
    elif 50 <= s <= 59: return "Retail & Wholesale"
    elif 70 <= s <= 89: return "Business Services"
    else: return "Other / Diversified"

df_sec["sector"] = df_sec["sic2"].apply(map_sector)
ct = pd.crosstab(df_sec["sector"], df_sec["archetype"])
```

- Technology is concentrated in Vocal Substantives (`{python} _rr("Technology", "Vocal Substantives")`× its index baseline; `{python} _ct("Technology", "Vocal Substantives")` of `{python} sec_n_arch["Vocal Substantives"]` firms). Technology providers have both the capability and the incentive to publicize customer-facing AI products.
- Financial Services (`{python} _rr("Financial Services", "Governance-Led Disclosers")`× overrepresented; `{python} _ct("Financial Services", "Governance-Led Disclosers")` firms), Utilities (`{python} _rr("Utilities", "Governance-Led Disclosers")`×), and Healthcare & Pharma (`{python} _rr("Healthcare & Pharma", "Governance-Led Disclosers")`×) dominate Governance-Led Disclosers. These heavily regulated sectors face strict compliance mandates, so ethical guardrails, model risk management, and oversight frameworks come first.
- Communications (`{python} _rr("Communications", "Defensive Disclosers")`×), Business Services (`{python} _rr("Business Services", "Defensive Disclosers")`×), Retail & Wholesale (`{python} _rr("Retail & Wholesale", "Defensive Disclosers")`×), and Industrials & Manufacturing (`{python} _rr("Industrials & Mfg", "Defensive Disclosers")`×) are overrepresented in Defensive Disclosers. Here AI is a competitive threat or a process change, not a revenue product.
- Energy & Mining (`{python} _rr("Energy & Mining", "No AI")`× overrepresented) and Industrials & Manufacturing (`{python} _rr("Industrials & Mfg", "No AI")`×) are the sectors most overrepresented among No AI firms, where digital transformation still takes a back seat to physical operations. Both sectors are small relative to the index, so together they make up only `{python} f"{(pct_col.loc['Energy & Mining', 'No AI'] + pct_col.loc['Industrials & Mfg', 'No AI']) * 100:.0f}"`% of the No AI group.

This is the sorting institutional theory predicts. Firms facing the same regulators and the same peers converge on the same disclosure register [@dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48; @suchman1995, pp. 571--74]. Posture is therefore partly an industry norm, not only a firm-level choice.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-representative-firms
#| tbl-cap: "Representative corporations across AI disclosure archetypes based on centroid distance and sectoral concentration. Centroid-closest firms are the five firms nearest to each archetype's mean standardized posture vector; dominant sectors are the largest sector shares within each archetype."
import numpy as np
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

_feat_cols = ["promotional_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation", "temporal_posture",
              "ai_positioning", "specificity", "disclosure_intensity"]
_fit = df_sec[df_sec["archetype"] != "No AI"].copy()
_zz = (_fit[_feat_cols] - _fit[_feat_cols].mean()) / _fit[_feat_cols].std()
_short = {"Technology": "Technology", "Financial Services": "Financial Services", "Healthcare & Pharma": "Healthcare & Pharma",
          "Industrials & Mfg": "Industrials & Mfg", "Retail & Wholesale": "Retail & Wholesale", "Utilities": "Utilities",
          "Communications": "Communications", "Energy & Mining": "Energy & Mining", "Business Services": "Business Services",
          "Transportation": "Transportation", "Other / Diversified": "Other / Diversified"}

def _clean_name(n):
    n = str(n)
    for suf in [", Inc.", " Inc.", " Inc", " Corporation", " Corp.", " Corp", " Company", " Co.", " plc", " PLC", " Holdings", " Ltd."]:
        n = n.replace(suf, "")
    return n.strip()

def _closest(a, k=5):
    idx = _fit.index[_fit["archetype"] == a]
    c = _zz.loc[idx].mean().values
    dist = np.linalg.norm(_zz.loc[idx].values - c, axis=1)
    best = idx[np.argsort(dist)[:k]]
    return ", ".join(f"{_clean_name(_fit.loc[i, 'company_name'])} (`{_fit.loc[i, 'ticker']}`)" for i in best)

def _dominant(a, k=3):
    s = (pct_col[a] * 100).sort_values(ascending=False).head(k)
    return ", ".join(f"{_short.get(i, i)} ({v:.1f}%)" for i, v in s.items())

_rows = [[f"**{a}**", _closest(a), _dominant(a)] for a in ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]]
_rows.append(["**No AI**", "Boundary threshold ($< 5$ frames)", _dominant("No AI")])
Markdown(tabulate(_rows, headers=["Archetype", "Closest-to-Centroid Examples", "Dominant Sectors"]))
```

Individual firms give the taxonomy face validity (@tbl-representative-firms). Beyond the centroid-closest firms, well-known Vocal Substantives include Microsoft, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, and Oracle. Governance-Led Disclosers include JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Apple, UnitedHealth, Walmart, and Chevron. Defensive Disclosers include Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Johnson & Johnson, Eli Lilly, Verizon, and Disney.

Two placements run against intuition. Apple sits with the Governance-Led group because its filings discuss AI mainly through oversight, privacy, and responsible-use language; product claims go to launches and marketing outside the SEC channel. Goldman Sachs sits with the Defensive group because its 10-K AI text is dominated by risk-factor language on model risk, competition, and regulation, with few concrete deployment claims. Both are classifications of what the firm writes, not of what it does.

Capital-intensive firms with little digital-transformation discourse, such as Costco, Texas Instruments, O'Reilly Automotive, and NVR, make up the No AI group. It also absorbs firms that left the index through acquisition or delisting before the generative-AI boom: `{python} int(df_sec.loc[df_sec["archetype"] == "No AI", "ticker"].isin(fu_delisted).sum())` of the `{python} int((df_sec["archetype"] == "No AI").sum())` No AI firms are delisted. They never had a post-2023 filing in which to adopt the new vocabulary. Keeping them avoids survivorship bias, but it means "No AI" partly reflects exit timing rather than a deliberate stance.

# From Disclosure Strategy to Disclosed AI Activity

## What corporate AI activity actually consists of

We now test whether the four disclosure archetypes line up with disclosed AI activity that was extracted on its own. Across `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` S&P 500 firms, the extraction finds `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` unique AI activity claims. For each one it records the action, the object, the business domain, the operational stage, the evidence strength, and the technology origin.

To make the activities readable for managers, we group them into six business roles:

- **Operate (Internal operations & workflows):** Optimizing supply chains, automating business processes, operational forecasting, logistics, and back-office financial administration.
- **Serve (Sales, marketing & client service):** Customer service chatbots, conversational client interfaces, recommendation engines, and targeted marketing.
- **Sell (Customer products & digital services):** Embedding AI capabilities, generative features, and predictive analytics directly into client-facing products and software solutions.
- **Enable (Employee productivity & software development):** Developer copilots, automated code generation, enterprise knowledge search, and internal employee tooling.
- **Control (Risk, cybersecurity & governance):** Real-time fraud detection, cybersecurity anomaly detection, compliance monitoring, and model risk oversight.
- **Build (Compute, data platforms & foundational models):** Enterprise data platforms, scalable cloud infrastructure, and training proprietary foundation models.

```{python}
#| label: fig-activity-map
#| fig-cap: "Corporate AI activity map: heatmap of disclosed AI activities across business purpose and operational action type."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 4.2
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))

def get_domain(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Customer products & services (Sell)"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Sales, marketing & service (Serve)"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Employee productivity & software (Enable)"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Risk, security & governance (Control)"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Data, compute & models (Build)"
    else:
        return "Internal operations & workflows (Operate)"

def get_action(row):
    a = str(row["action"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    if a in ["deploy", "scale", "integrate"]:
        if "automation" in obj:
            return "Automate"
        return "Deploy / Integrate"
    elif a in ["develop", "invest_infrastructure"]:
        return "Develop / Build"
    elif a in ["partner", "buy_or_license"]:
        return "Partner / Buy"
    elif a in ["pilot_or_explore"]:
        return "Pilot / Explore"
    elif a in ["measure_outcome"]:
        return "Analyze / Measure"
    elif a in ["govern_or_control", "restrict"]:
        return "Govern / Control"
    return "Deploy / Integrate"

df["domain_clean"] = df.apply(get_domain, axis=1)
df["action_clean"] = df.apply(get_action, axis=1)

rows_order = [
    "Customer products & services (Sell)",
    "Internal operations & workflows (Operate)",
    "Data, compute & models (Build)",
    "Employee productivity & software (Enable)",
    "Risk, security & governance (Control)",
    "Sales, marketing & service (Serve)"
]
cols_order = [
    "Deploy / Integrate",
    "Develop / Build",
    "Partner / Buy",
    "Pilot / Explore",
    "Analyze / Measure",
    "Automate",
    "Govern / Control"
]

ct_raw = pd.crosstab(df["domain_clean"], df["action_clean"]).reindex(index=rows_order, columns=cols_order).fillna(0)
row_pct = ct_raw.div(ct_raw.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
total_acts = ct_raw.values.sum()

row_labels = [
    f"{r}\n[n = {int(ct_raw.loc[r].sum()):,}; {ct_raw.loc[r].sum()/total_acts*100:.1f}% AI acts]"
    for r in rows_order
]
col_labels = [
    f"{c}\n[n = {int(ct_raw[c].sum()):,}; {ct_raw[c].sum()/total_acts*100:.1f}% AI acts]"
    for c in cols_order
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.8, 4.8), dpi=300)
im = ax.imshow(row_pct.values, cmap="Blues", aspect="auto", vmin=0, vmax=90)

ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols_order)))
ax.set_xticklabels(col_labels, fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold", rotation=25, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows_order)))
ax.set_yticklabels(row_labels, fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold")

for i in range(len(rows_order)):
    for j in range(len(cols_order)):
        val = int(ct_raw.iloc[i, j])
        r_pct = row_pct.iloc[i, j]
        text_color = "white" if r_pct > 45 else "#0F172A"
        ax.text(j, i, f"{val:,}\n({r_pct:.1f}%)", ha="center", va="center",
                color=text_color, fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold" if r_pct > 15 else "normal")

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.04)
cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
cbar.set_label("Row implementation share (% within Business Purpose AI activities)", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_title(f"Corporate AI Activity Map: Business Purpose × Action Type (n = {int(total_acts):,} AI activities)\n[Cells report counts and row percentages; row percentages sum to 100% across action types]",
             fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Corporate AI is mostly an application-layer story (@fig-activity-map). S&P 500 firms describe deploying and integrating commercial AI tools into the products and workflows they already have. Developing foundation models or building core computing infrastructure is a negligible fraction of total activity.

## Disclosure strategy meets disclosed AI activity

The central test links communication posture to disclosed AI activity. The activity inventory was never an input to the clustering; the archetypes come strictly from frame-level communication posture.

Cross-tabulating the archetypes against activity characteristics shows that posture maps directly onto operational disclosure (@fig-archetype-activity-heatmap and @tbl-4-1-archetype-profile):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-activity-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Disclosed AI activity profile across communication archetypes. Cell values report raw activity rates; shading indicates standardized intensity across archetypes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.0
#| fig-height: 3.8
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(df_strat[["ticker", "archetype"]], on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]
n_activities = act.groupby("ticker").size()
per_firm = df_strat.set_index("ticker")["archetype"].to_frame().join(n_activities.rename("n_activities")).fillna(0)

act["proprietary_ai"] = (act["action"] == "develop") | (act["ai_source"] == "own")
act["own_brand_named"] = act["own_brands"].map(lambda v: len(v) > 0)
act["quantified_outcome"] = (act["action"] == "measure_outcome") | (act["evidence_strength"] == "metric")
act["deployed_or_scaled"] = act["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])
act["customer_target"] = act["target"] == "customers"

act_features = [
    ("Median AI activities / firm", [per_firm[per_firm.archetype == a]["n_activities"].median() for a in ARCH]),
    ("Proprietary AI share (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["proprietary_ai"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Own brand named (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["own_brand_named"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Customer-facing share (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["customer_target"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Deployed / scaled (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["deployed_or_scaled"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Quantified metric (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["quantified_outcome"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH])
]

mat_act = np.array([vals for _, vals in act_features])
mat_act_z = (mat_act - mat_act.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / (mat_act.std(axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2), dpi=300)
vmax = float(np.abs(mat_act_z).max())
im = ax.imshow(mat_act_z, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto")

ax.set_xticks(range(3))
ax.set_xticklabels(ARCH, fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", rotation=30, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(act_features)))
ax.set_yticklabels([name for name, _ in act_features], fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")

for i in range(len(act_features)):
    for j in range(3):
        raw_v = mat_act[i, j]
        z_v = mat_act_z[i, j]
        fmt_val = f"{raw_v:.0f}" if i == 0 else f"{raw_v:.1f}%"
        ax.text(j, i, fmt_val, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
                color="white" if abs(z_v) > vmax * 0.55 else "#0F172A")

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.85, pad=0.03)
cbar.set_label("Standardized difference (z-score)", fontsize=8.0)
ax.set_title("Disclosed AI Activity Profile Across Communication Archetypes",
             fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
