```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1-archetype-profile
#| tbl-cap: "Disclosed AI activity profile by disclosure archetype, from the disclosed AI activity inventory (never an input to the posture clustering)."
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))[["ticker", "archetype"]]
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(strat, on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers", "No AI"]
n_firms = strat["archetype"].value_counts()
n_activities = act.groupby("ticker").size()
per_firm = strat.set_index("ticker")["archetype"].to_frame().join(n_activities.rename("n_activities")).fillna(0)

def share(col):
    return [f"{act[act.archetype == a][col].mean() * 100:.1f}%" for a in ARCH]

act["proprietary_ai"] = (act["action"] == "develop") | (act["ai_source"] == "own")
act["own_brand_named"] = act["own_brands"].map(lambda v: len(v) > 0)
act["quantified_outcome"] = (act["action"] == "measure_outcome") | (act["evidence_strength"] == "metric")
act["deployed_or_scaled"] = act["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])
act["customer_target"] = act["target"] == "customers"

rows = [
    ["Disclosed AI activities per firm (median)"] + [f"{per_firm[per_firm.archetype == a]['n_activities'].median():.0f}" for a in ARCH],
    ["Customer-facing AI activity share (%)"] + share("customer_target"),
    ["Technology source: proprietary/own (%)"] + share("proprietary_ai"),
    ["AI activities naming an own product/brand (%)"] + share("own_brand_named"),
    ["AI activities reporting a quantified outcome (%)"] + share("quantified_outcome"),
    ["AI activities at stage deployed/scaled (%)"] + share("deployed_or_scaled"),
]
headers = ["AI activity feature"] + [f"{a} (n={n_firms[a]})" for a in ARCH]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=headers))
```

*Notes:* Distributions computed from the `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"`-AI-activity inventory (`{python} hd_n_activity_firms` firms with at least one disclosed AI activity out of the `{python} hd_n_universe`-firm universe), joined post hoc to the posture-based archetype assignment. Column headers give the number of firms per archetype in the full universe, so firms without any activity contribute zeros. "No AI" firms with positive activity counts reflect conference-call statements by firms whose formal SEC filings omit AI entirely. Full 14-variable AI activity profile reported in @tbl-a4-full-archetype-profile (Appendix C).

Vocal Substantives lead on every operational-depth dimension: more AI activities, more proprietary technology, more customer-facing deployment, and more production-stage systems. Governance-Led Disclosers sit in the middle. Defensive Disclosers report the thinnest and least mature inventory.

Frames and activities come from the same corporate text, so the activity gap could simply reflect that some firms write more. To rule out this shared-source confound, we estimate a negative binomial regression of disclosed AI activity counts on the archetypes, conditioning on total AI disclosure volume ($\log(1 + \text{AI frames})$):

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[\text{AI Activities}_i] = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{VocalSubstantives}_i + \beta_2 \text{GovernanceLed}_i + \gamma \log(1 + \text{Frames}_i)
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1b-volume-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: "Disclosed AI activity count by archetype, before and after conditioning on total AI disclosure volume (log frame count). Reference category: Defensive Disclosers."
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

reg = json.loads(_p("strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())["activity_volume_regression"]
OTHERS = ["Governance-Led Disclosers", "Vocal Substantives"]

def fmt_p(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

rows = [[a, f"{reg['raw'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['raw'][a]['p']),
        f"{reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['p'])] for a in OTHERS]
rows.append(["log(1 + AI frames)", "-", "-", f"{reg['log_frames_coef']:+.2f} (coef.)", fmt_p(reg['log_frames_p'])])
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=[f"Archetype vs. {reg['reference']}", "Raw ratio", "p", "Volume-adjusted ratio", "p"]))
```

A real difference survives the volume control. At the same total disclosure volume, Vocal Substantives still report `{python} f"{hd_vs_ratio:.2f}"` times as many AI activities as Defensive Disclosers ($p < 0.001$), and Governance-Led Disclosers report `{python} f"{hd_gl_ratio:.2f}"` times as many ($p < 0.001$). Volume does explain most of the raw gap, as the shared-source concern predicts: log frame count alone accounts for a pseudo-$R^2$ of `{python} f"{hd_vol_r2:.2f}"` in the adjusted model. Posture is not just verbosity; it reflects different intensities of disclosed AI activity.

## What firms actually do differently

The archetypes differ not only in how many activities they disclose but in what those activities are for (@fig-archetype-activity-mix):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-activity-mix
#| fig-cap: "Mix of disclosed corporate AI activities by disclosure archetype (100% stacked horizontal bars). Vocal Substantives dedicate over 60% of AI activities to client products (Sell); Governance-Led prioritize internal operations (Operate) and governance control (Control)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 3.6
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(df_strat[["ticker", "archetype"]], on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

def get_role(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Sell (Customer products)"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Serve (Sales & service)"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Enable (Productivity & dev)"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Control (Risk & security)"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Build (Compute & data)"
    else:
        return "Operate (Internal operations)"

act["role"] = act.apply(get_role, axis=1)
ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]
ct_mix = pd.crosstab(act["archetype"], act["role"], normalize="index") * 100

roles_order = [
    "Sell (Customer products)",
    "Operate (Internal operations)",
    "Build (Compute & data)",
    "Enable (Productivity & dev)",
    "Control (Risk & security)",
    "Serve (Sales & service)"
]
colors = ["#1D4ED8", "#0D9488", "#D97706", "#6366F1", "#DC2626", "#E11D48"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 3.6), dpi=300)
y_pos = np.arange(3)
left = np.zeros(3)

for role, col in zip(roles_order, colors):
    vals = [ct_mix.loc[a, role] for a in ARCH]
    bars = ax.barh(y_pos, vals, left=left, color=col, edgecolor="white", height=0.55, label=role)
    for idx, (b, v) in enumerate(zip(bars, vals)):
        if v >= 6.0:
            ax.text(left[idx] + v/2, b.get_y() + b.get_height()/2, f"{v:.1f}%",
                    ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold")
    left += vals

ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels(ARCH, fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("% of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_title("Mix of Disclosed Corporate AI Activities by Disclosure Archetype (100% Stacked)",
             fontsize=10.0, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), loc="upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=8.0, frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The stacked mix in @fig-archetype-activity-mix shows where AI enters each type of firm:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
def _mix(a, role):
    return f"{ct_mix.loc[a, role]:.1f}"
_SELL, _OPER, _CTRL, _SERVE = "Sell (Customer products)", "Operate (Internal operations)", "Control (Risk & security)", "Serve (Sales & service)"
```

1. **Vocal Substantives focus on revenue-generating products:** Most of their disclosed AI activities (`{python} _mix("Vocal Substantives", _SELL)`%) fall under Sell, embedding AI directly into customer products and services, while internal operations account for only `{python} _mix("Vocal Substantives", _OPER)`%.
2. **Governance-Led Disclosers tilt toward internal operations:** Their mix splits almost evenly between Operate (`{python} _mix("Governance-Led Disclosers", _OPER)`%) and Sell (`{python} _mix("Governance-Led Disclosers", _SELL)`%), the most balanced of the three groups. Control activities (risk, fraud detection, model governance) stay a small share (`{python} _mix("Governance-Led Disclosers", _CTRL)`%) even here, far from the governance emphasis of their filing language. Governance is how these firms talk, not mainly what they do.
3. **Defensive Disclosers describe the same commercial and operational uses as everyone else, only fewer of them:** Their activities split between Sell (`{python} _mix("Defensive Disclosers", _SELL)`%) and Operate (`{python} _mix("Defensive Disclosers", _OPER)`%), with Serve (customer-service bots) at `{python} _mix("Defensive Disclosers", _SERVE)`%. What sets this group apart is low volume, not a different kind of activity.

Sell dominates the mix in all three groups. The archetypes differ in how strongly (Vocal Substantives most of all) and in how much they disclose, not in what corporate AI is for.

## Decomposing AI activity grounding

Firms disclose thousands of AI activities, but the question that matters is how concretely each one is grounded in the text. To measure AI activity grounding ($G$), we pass all `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` disclosed activities through a ladder of increasingly demanding requirements:

$$\text{AI Activity Claim} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Specific Business Function} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Deployed Stage} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Named Product/Process} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Quantified Outcome Metric}$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-ladder-substance
#| fig-cap: "Decomposing AI activity grounding: cumulative nested progression of evidence requirements (left) and independent grounding attribute frequencies (right) across all disclosed AI activities."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.8
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data_path = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not data_path.exists():
    data_path = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")

df = pd.read_parquet(data_path)
n_total = len(df)

# Nested counts
c1 = n_total
c2 = len(df[df["function_family"] != "unspecified"])
c3 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])])
c4 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & df["evidence_strength"].isin(["named_product_or_process", "metric"])])
c5 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & (df["evidence_strength"] == "metric")])

pcts_nested = [c / n_total * 100 for c in [c1, c2, c3, c4, c5]]

# Independent component rates
p_func = (df["function_family"] != "unspecified").mean() * 100
p_stage = df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]).mean() * 100
p_named = df["evidence_strength"].isin(["named_product_or_process", "metric"]).mean() * 100
p_metric = (df["evidence_strength"] == "metric").mean() * 100
p_vendor = (df["ai_source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), dpi=300)

labels_nested = [
    "1. Discloses an AI activity claim",
    "2. + Specific business function",
    "3. + Deployed / scaled stage",
    "4. + Named product or process",
    "5. + Quantified outcome / metric"
]
colors_nested = ["#94A3B8", "#64748B", "#3B82F6", "#2563EB", "#1D4ED8"]
bars1 = ax1.barh(labels_nested[::-1], pcts_nested[::-1], color=colors_nested[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars1, pcts_nested[::-1]):
    ax1.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax1.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax1.set_xlabel(f"% of all {n_total:,} disclosed AI activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_title("Decomposing AI Activity Grounding\n(Strictly Nested Concreteness Requirements)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

labels_ind = [
    "Deployed or scaled stage",
    "Specific business function",
    "Named product or process",
    "Quantified outcome metric",
    "External vendor / model attributed"
]
pcts_ind = [p_stage, p_func, p_named, p_metric, p_vendor]
colors_ind = ["#059669", "#0284C7", "#6366F1", "#D97706", "#DC2626"]
bars2 = ax2.barh(labels_ind[::-1], pcts_ind[::-1], color=colors_ind[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars2, pcts_ind[::-1]):
    ax2.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax2.set_xlabel("% of AI activities with attribute present", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_title("Independent AI Grounding Attributes\n(% of AI activities meeting each criterion)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Only `{python} f"{c5 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% of disclosed AI activities reach the top of the ladder, pairing an operational deployment with a quantified performance metric (@fig-ladder-substance). The drop is steep: `{python} f"{c2 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% specify a business function and `{python} f"{c3 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% are both function-specific and deployed or scaled, but the share that also names a tangible product, process, or metric falls to `{python} f"{c4 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`%. Most disclosed AI activities are hard to evaluate from outside because they come with no quantified outcome.

## The paradox of the GenAI boom

The generative-AI boom multiplied the volume of disclosed AI activity and lowered its average grounding. Between 2021 and 2026 the number of disclosed activities per year rose several-fold. Over the same period three grounding shares fell (@fig-volume-vs-grounding). Fewer activities were at a deployed or scaled stage, fewer named a specific product or process, and fewer had an identified business function. The marginal activity added after 2023 is, on average, less concrete than what firms were already disclosing.

This is what H1 anticipates. Once a vocabulary becomes an institutional expectation, the language spreads faster than the grounded activity behind it [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41]. Activity counts accumulate over the year, so the 2026 volume is shown both as observed year to date and as a full-year estimate using the same-window seasonal factor. The 2026 grounding shares are rates and are read as observed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-volume-vs-grounding
#| fig-cap: "The paradox of the GenAI boom: disclosed AI activity volume surged several-fold (Panel A), while marginal concreteness and grounding indicators deteriorated (Panel B), 2021–2025 (2026 shown as year-to-date)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.8
#| fig-height: 4.0
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import duckdb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

db_path = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not db_path.exists():
    db_path = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
act_path = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not act_path.exists():
    act_path = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")

act = pd.read_parquet(act_path)
con = duckdb.connect(str(db_path), read_only=True)
filings = con.execute("""
    WITH manifest AS (
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest WHERE form_type != 'Earnings call transcript'
        UNION ALL
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q
    )
    SELECT accession_number, filing_date FROM manifest
""").df()
con.close()

act_f = act[act.channel == "filing"].merge(filings, on="accession_number", how="left")
act_f["year"] = pd.to_datetime(act_f["filing_date"]).dt.year
act_c = act[act.channel == "call"].copy()
act_c["year"] = act_c["accession_number"].str.extract(r"_(\d{4})Q")[0].astype(float)
both = pd.concat([act_f, act_c], ignore_index=True)
both = both[both["year"].between(2021, 2026)]
both["year"] = both["year"].astype(int)

vol = both.groupby("year").size()
dep_share = both.groupby("year")["stage"].apply(lambda s: s.isin(["deployed", "scaled"]).mean() * 100)
gen_ev = both.groupby("year")["evidence_strength"].apply(lambda s: (s == "generic").mean() * 100)
named_prod = both.groupby("year")["evidence_strength"].apply(lambda s: (s == "named_product_or_process").mean() * 100)
ident_func = both.groupby("year")["function_family"].apply(lambda s: (s != "unspecified").mean() * 100)

# Full-year 2026 projection with the same-window seasonal factor (activities
# in full 2025 / activities in the 2025 window ending on the 2026 cut-off day),
# computed once in the header chunk as hd_act_factor.
latest_date_2026 = act_f[act_f["year"] == 2026]["filing_date"].max()
months_observed = latest_date_2026.month if pd.notnull(latest_date_2026) else 8
annual_factor = hd_act_factor
vol_2026_obs = vol[2026]
vol_2026_proj_total = int(round(vol_2026_obs * annual_factor))
vol_2026_proj_adj = vol_2026_proj_total - vol_2026_obs

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 4.2), dpi=300)

years = sorted(vol.index.tolist())
main_years = [y for y in years if y <= 2025]
ytd_years = [y for y in years if y >= 2025]

# Panel A: Total Disclosed Corporate AI Activities with Stacked Year-End Projection
bars_hist = ax1.bar(main_years, [vol[y] for y in main_years], color="#2563EB", width=0.55, edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, label="Observed full-year AI activities")
bar_26_obs = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_obs], color="#60A5FA", width=0.55, edgecolor="#2563EB", lw=1.2, label="2026 YTD observed AI activities")
bar_26_proj = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_proj_adj], bottom=[vol_2026_obs], color="#DBEAFE", width=0.55,
                      edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, linestyle="--", hatch="///", label="Projected year-end AI activity adjustment")

max_v = max(max(vol[y] for y in main_years), vol_2026_proj_total)
ax1.set_ylim(0, max_v * 1.20)

for y in main_years:
    v = vol[y]
    ax1.text(y, v + max_v * 0.02, f"{v:,}", ha="center", fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")

ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_obs * 0.55, f"{vol_2026_obs:,}\n(YTD)", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold", color="#1E3A8A")
ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_proj_total + max_v * 0.02, f"{vol_2026_proj_total:,}\n(FY Proj.)", ha="center", fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold", color="#1D4ED8")

ax1.set_ylabel("Number of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xticks(years)
ax1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.2, framealpha=0.9)
growth_ratio = vol[2025] / vol[2021]
proj_ratio = vol_2026_proj_total / vol[2021]
ax1.set_title(f"Panel A: AI Activity Volume Surges ({growth_ratio:.1f}× panel, {proj_ratio:.1f}× proj.)\nTotal Disclosed Corporate AI Activities", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens
def _trend_label(base, series):
    return f"{base} ({series[main_years[0]]:.0f}% → {series[main_years[-1]]:.0f}%)"

ax2.plot(main_years, [dep_share[y] for y in main_years], "o-", color="#059669", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Deployed or scaled", dep_share))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [dep_share[y] for y in ytd_years], "o:", color="#059669", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [ident_func[y] for y in main_years], "s-", color="#0284C7", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Identifiable business function", ident_func))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [ident_func[y] for y in ytd_years], "s:", color="#0284C7", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [named_prod[y] for y in main_years], "^-", color="#6366F1", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Named product or process", named_prod))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [named_prod[y] for y in ytd_years], "^:", color="#6366F1", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in main_years], "d--", color="#DC2626", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Generic, unanchored evidence", gen_ev))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in ytd_years], "d:", color="#DC2626", lw=1.8, ms=5)

all_shares = pd.concat([dep_share, ident_func, named_prod, gen_ev])
min_s, max_s = all_shares.min(), all_shares.max()
s_range = max_s - min_s
ax2.set_ylim(max(0, min_s - s_range * 0.15), min(100, max_s + s_range * 0.40))
ax2.set_ylabel("Share of Disclosed AI Activities (%)", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xticks(years)
ax2.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="upper right", framealpha=0.92)
ax2.set_title("Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens\nGrounding and Specificity Indicators Over Time", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("The Paradox of the GenAI Boom: Disclosed AI Activity Expanded Faster than Observable Grounding",
             fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", y=0.98)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.94])
plt.show()
```

The magnitudes are large. Disclosed activities in 2025, the last complete year, were `{python} f"{growth_ratio:.1f}"` times the 2021 count. The full-year 2026 estimate (seasonal factor `{python} f"{hd_act_factor:.2f}"`, the ratio of full-year to same-window activity in 2025) reaches `{python} f"{proj_ratio:.1f}"` times the 2021 count. Over 2021–2025 the share at a deployed or scaled stage fell from `{python} f"{dep_share[main_years[0]]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{dep_share[main_years[-1]]:.0f}"`% (`{python} f"{dep_share[2026]:.0f}"`% in 2026 year to date). The share naming a specific product or process fell from `{python} f"{named_prod[main_years[0]]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{named_prod[main_years[-1]]:.0f}"`% (`{python} f"{named_prod[2026]:.0f}"`% in 2026). This is a fact about information, not about capabilities: we do not claim that firms got worse at AI. The marginal AI activity disclosed after ChatGPT was less concrete, less mature, and more speculative than what came before it.

## Who owns the AI

Investors and regulators reading AI claims also want to know where the technology comes from: whether public firms build it themselves or buy foundation models from third-party hyperscalers.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))
n_activities_total = len(df)

def check_role(entities, roles):
    if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
        return False
    return any(e.get("role") in roles for e in entities)

own_brand_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["own_product_or_brand"])).mean() * 100
ext_vendor_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["external_provider", "external_model"])).mean() * 100
partner_pct = df["named_entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["partner"])).mean() * 100
third_party_src = (df["ai_source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100
any_ext_provider = df.groupby("ticker")["named_entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["external_provider", "external_model", "partner"])).any())
ext_provider_firm_pct = 100 * any_ext_provider.mean()

_VENDOR_PATTERNS = {
    "OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem": r"openai|chatgpt|gpt|copilot|microsoft|azure",
    "Alphabet / Google": r"google|gemini|vertex|bard|deepmind|palm",
    "NVIDIA": r"nvidia|cuda",
    "Amazon Web Services": r"amazon|aws|bedrock|sagemaker",
}

def _vendor_firm_pct(pattern):
    import re
    def has_vendor(entities):
        if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
            return False
        return any(e.get("role") in ("external_provider", "external_model", "partner") and re.search(pattern, str(e.get("name", "")).lower()) for e in entities)
    by_firm = df.groupby("ticker")["named_entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(has_vendor).any())
    return 100 * by_firm.mean()

vendor_pcts = {name: _vendor_firm_pct(pat) for name, pat in _VENDOR_PATTERNS.items()}
```

Named entity roles across the `{python} f"{n_activities_total:,}"` disclosed AI activity statements show a clear provenance asymmetry (@fig-tech-provenance):

- `{python} f"{own_brand_pct:.1f}"`% of all disclosed AI activity statements attach a proprietary corporate brand or in-house product name to the deployment.
- `{python} f"{ext_vendor_pct:.1f}"`% cite an external technology vendor or foundation model (and `{python} f"{partner_pct:.1f}"`% name a commercial partner).
- This is despite `{python} f"{ext_provider_firm_pct:.1f}"`% of S&P 500 firms naming at least one external technology provider, model family, or hyperscaler somewhere in their disclosures.

### Regional orientation of AI disclosure

A related question is the regional orientation of AI disclosure: when S&P 500 firms discuss AI, which geographic ecosystems (technology providers, but also markets, competitors, and regulators) do they talk about?

We measure it with a lexical taxonomy applied only inside AI-context text, that is, paragraphs that already carry an extracted AI disclosure frame. A mention is any word-boundary match, inside such a paragraph, of a term mapped to a region in the taxonomy. Terms are named technology entities (foundation models, hyperscalers, chipmakers, enterprise platforms) plus literal country and demonym terms (e.g. "China," "Chinese," "Japan"). Because the scan stays inside AI paragraphs, a mention never comes from an unrelated supply-chain or tariff risk factor that happens to name a country. Regions are United States, Europe, China, and Other (the full term list is in Appendix C).

The United States is measured asymmetrically. Only named technology entities count (e.g. "OpenAI," "NVIDIA"), never the literal country name. Every U.S.-domiciled filer names its own jurisdiction all the time, and a literal match would saturate the U.S. share. Every other region is matched by both named entities and literal country/demonym terms, so the United States share below is, if anything, understated.

## External characterization of archetypes: fundamental financial profiles

Financial fundamentals and market prices do not come from disclosure text; they come from XBRL filings and market returns. We test whether the archetypes correspond to economically distinct firms, first on raw medians and then after sector-by-year adjustment ($X = \alpha_{s,y} + \gamma \cdot \text{Archetype} + \varepsilon$, referenced against No AI, with firm-clustered standard errors).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_econ = json.loads(_p("strategy_economic_profiles.json").read_text())
econ_a = _econ["panel_a"]
d = _econ["panel_b"]

def _pfmt(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"= {p:.3g}"

def _reg(key, seg):
    row = d[key][seg]
    return row["gamma"], row["se"], row["p"]

vs_mktcap_g, _, vs_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_rd_g, _, vs_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_gm_g, _, vs_gm_p = _reg("gross_margin", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_beta_g, _, vs_beta_p = _reg("beta", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_ps_g, _, vs_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Vocal Substantives")

gov_mktcap_g, _, gov_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_roic_g, _, gov_roic_p = _reg("roic_minus_wacc", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_ps_g, _, gov_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Governance-Led Disclosers")

def_rd_g, _, def_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Defensive Disclosers")

rd_vs, rd_gov, rd_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"]
gm_vs, gm_gov, gm_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["gross_margin"]
beta_vs, beta_gov, beta_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["beta"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["beta"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["beta"]
```

Raw medians already put Vocal Substantives ahead of the other two archetypes on the dimensions that matter for a technology-intensive segment: R&D/sales `{python} f"{100*rd_vs:.1f}"`% vs. `{python} f"{100*min(rd_gov, rd_def):.1f}"`–`{python} f"{100*max(rd_gov, rd_def):.1f}"`% for the other archetypes, gross margin `{python} f"{100*gm_vs:.1f}"`% vs. `{python} f"{100*min(gm_gov, gm_def):.1f}"`–`{python} f"{100*max(gm_gov, gm_def):.1f}"`%, beta `{python} f"{beta_vs:.2f}"` vs. `{python} f"{min(beta_gov, beta_def):.2f}"`–`{python} f"{max(beta_gov, beta_def):.2f}"`. The sector-year-adjusted panel confirms each archetype separately:

- **Vocal Substantives** is the most consistently distinct archetype. It carries `{python} f"{vs_mktcap_g:+.2f}"` log points of market cap ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_mktcap_p)`) and `{python} f"{100*vs_rd_g:+.1f}"` percentage points of R&D-to-sales ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_rd_p)`). It also carries `{python} f"{100*vs_gm_g:+.1f}"` points of gross margin ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_gm_p)`), `{python} f"{vs_beta_g:+.2f}"` of beta ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_beta_p)`), and `{python} f"{vs_ps_g:+.2f}"` of price-to-sales ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_ps_p)`).
- **Governance-Led Disclosers** separate from No AI mainly on scale and earnings quality, not technology intensity. They show a market-cap premium (`{python} f"{gov_mktcap_g:+.2f}"` log points, $p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_mktcap_p)`) and a ROIC-minus-WACC premium (`{python} f"{gov_roic_g:+.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_roic_p)`). Their price-to-sales effect, by contrast, is `{python} f"{gov_ps_g:+.2f}"` ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(gov_ps_p)`). This fits an archetype defined by governance-heavy disclosure that tracks firm size and regulatory exposure (larger, more regulated firms write more governance content), not distinctive AI economics.
- **Defensive Disclosers** separate least from No AI: an R&D effect of `{python} f"{100*def_rd_g:+.1f}"` points ($p$ `{python} _pfmt(def_rd_p)`) is the most notable dimension.

After sector-year adjustment, the archetype most grounded in disclosed AI activity (Vocal Substantives, @tbl-4-1-archetype-profile) is also the one most consistently distinct on fundamentals. Talking about AI, or stressing governance, is not by itself tied to distinctive economics. This is what signalling theory predicts [@spence1973, pp. 363--64]: the market-relevant information sits in the costly, specific content of disclosure, not in its volume or register.

```{python}
#| label: fig-economic-coefficients
#| fig-cap: "Sector-year-adjusted effect of disclosure archetype on firm fundamentals, relative to No AI (95% CI, firm-clustered SE). Vocal Substantives separates most consistently from the sector-year baseline."

ax.axvline(0, color="#334155", lw=1)
```

## What disclosed AI activity adds to disclosure posture

Disclosed activity carries information that posture alone does not, and that settles H2. At equal disclosure volume, Vocal Substantives report `{python} f"{hd_vs_ratio:.2f}"` times as many AI activities as Defensive Disclosers, so the archetypes are not a proxy for verbosity. What firms report doing is the same everywhere (selling and operating with AI), and only the archetype that pairs promotion with grounded activity stands out on sector-year-adjusted fundamentals. For an investor or issuer, archetype membership is a first screen. The information sits in the grounding attributes of the individual activities, which feed the credibility tests that follow.

# Credibility Under Increasing Disclosure Commitment

There is no audited census of corporate AI deployment, so we define credibility by what survives as disclosure becomes more costly to commit to [@crawford1982, pp. 1431--32; @rogers2011, pp. 2155--56]. The credibility ladder in @fig-credibility-ladder orders those commitments. Its first three rungs (named artifacts, deployment stage, quantified outcomes) are the components of AI Activity Grounding and are tested jointly through Decoupling ($W$). The last two, survival of claims across venues and response to direct SEC scrutiny, each get their own design.

## Empirical credibility tests: the credibility ladder

```{python}
#| label: fig-credibility-ladder
#| fig-cap: "The credibility ladder: escalating verification cost and disclosure commitment across corporate communication layers."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.2), dpi=300)
ax.axis('off')

steps = [
    ('NARRATIVE CLAIM', 'Surface talk (AI frames, promotional sentiment)', '#E2E8F0', '#475569'),
    ('DISCLOSED SUBSTANCE', 'Operational AI activities (specific actions & objects)', '#CBD5E1', '#334155'),
    ('EVIDENCE ATTACHED', 'Concrete attributes (quantified metrics, named partners/tools)', '#93C5FD', '#1E40AF'),
    ('EVIDENCE SURVIVES FORMAL VENUE', 'Cross-venue persistence (filing retains earnings call claims)', '#60A5FA', '#1D4ED8'),
    ('DISCLOSURE RESPONDS TO SCRUTINY', 'Disciplining under regulatory enforcement (SEC shock)', '#2563EB', '#FFFFFF'),
]

n = len(steps)
for i, (title, sub, bg, fg) in enumerate(steps):
    y = n - 1 - i
    rect = patches.FancyBboxPatch((0.15, y * 0.9), 0.65, 0.65, boxstyle='round,pad=0.04',
                                  facecolor=bg, edgecolor='#94A3B8', lw=1.2)
    ax.add_patch(rect)
    ax.text(0.475, y * 0.9 + 0.40, title, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9.0, fontweight='bold', color=fg if fg == '#FFFFFF' else '#0F172A')
    ax.text(0.475, y * 0.9 + 0.18, sub, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, color=fg if fg == '#FFFFFF' else '#475569')
    
    if i < n - 1:
        ax.annotate('', xy=(0.475, y * 0.9), xytext=(0.475, y * 0.9 - 0.25),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='<-', lw=1.5, color='#64748B'))

# Right side progression arrow
ax.annotate('', xy=(0.88, 0.2), xytext=(0.88, 4.2),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='<-', lw=2.0, color='#0F172A', mutation_scale=15))
ax.text(0.92, 2.2, 'Increasing disclosure commitment &\nverification cost \u2192', rotation=-90,
        ha='left', va='center', fontsize=8.5, fontweight='bold', color='#0F172A')

ax.set_xlim(0.05, 1.05)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 4.6)
```

## Where disclosure runs ahead of substance

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def _p(name):

    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_df_w = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))

_validation = json.loads(_p("washing_score_validation.json").read_text())

n_firms_panel = _validation["n_firms"]
year_min, year_max = int(_df_w["year"].min()), int(_df_w["year"].max())
```

We ask whether a firm's disclosure volume keeps pace with its concrete operational substance. Volume is Disclosure Intensity ($D$: AI frames per thousand words); substance is Disclosed Substance ($S$: log activity count weighted by AI Activity Grounding). The sample is `{python} f"{n_firm_years:,}"` disclosing firm-years (`{python} n_firms_panel` S&P 500 firms, `{python} year_min`–`{python} year_max`, `{python} year_max` shown as year-to-date). Decoupling ($W_{it}$) is the signed difference between the percentile ranks of Disclosure Intensity ($D_{it}$) and Disclosed Substance ($S_{it}$):
$$
W_{it} = \text{pct\_rank}(D_{it}) - \text{pct\_rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]
$$
By construction, $W = 0$ means talk and substance rank the same, $W > 0$ means narrative runs ahead of grounded substance ("decoupling"), and $W < 0$ means "quiet substance."


## What changes from filing to call

If decoupling is a lasting posture, what happens when the same firm discusses AI in two venues with very different legal liability?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

grounding = json.loads(_p("activity_grounding.json").read_text())
gap = grounding["channel_gap"]
gap_n_cells, gap_n_firms = gap["n_cells"], gap["n_firms"]
```

We test this with a firm × fiscal-year fixed effects design ($\alpha_{i,t}$) across `{python} gap_n_cells` balanced firm-year cells (`{python} gap_n_firms` firms) with $\ge 3$ disclosed AI activities in both channels:

$$
Y_{i,t,\text{venue}} = \alpha_{i,t} + \beta \, \mathbf{1}[\text{venue} = \text{Call}] + \varepsilon_{i,t,\text{venue}}
$$

Each cell has exactly two observations. All of the firm's earnings calls in the fiscal year are pooled into one call observation. All of its statutory SEC filings (10-K and 10-Qs) are pooled into one filing observation. Each is expressed per thousand words or as a share of that venue's activities. The estimator measures the within-firm, within-period venue-associated difference ($\text{Call}_{i,t} - \text{Filing}_{i,t}$), with standard errors clustered by firm. This sweeps out time-invariant firm unobservables, business models, and macroeconomic conditions.

It does not sweep out features of the venue itself, such as the question-and-answer format of calls or analyst prompting. The coefficient is therefore a venue difference, not a causal effect of legal liability. Because the sample requires at least three disclosed activities in both venues, it over-represents heavier AI disclosers relative to the index.

What firms claim to do is the same in both venues; the evidence they attach to it is not (@fig-venue-call-filing-differences).

```{python}
#| label: fig-venue-call-filing-differences

Panel A demonstrates that core AI activity shares are preserved across venues. Panel B shows that statutory filings (10-K and 10-Q) contain substantially fewer evidentiary details per activity. Both panels are firm × fiscal-year fixed-effects estimates; the pooled call/filing ratios reported elsewhere are descriptive means without fixed effects."

    return gap, gap - 1.96 * se, gap + 1.96 * se, p

for i, d in enumerate(diffs1):

ax1.set_yticks(y1)

for i, d in enumerate(diffs2):
```

In Panel B, the evidence attached to those activities is a different story:

- **Named business function:** `{python} b_function`.
- **Quantified outcome or performance metric:** `{python} b_quant`.
- **Named third-party provider or vendor:** `{python} b_provider`.
- **Named product or process:** `{python} b_product`.
- **Governance caveats and restrictions:** `{python} b_governance`.

> The AI activity story is the same in both venues; the evidence behind it gets thinner in the one that binds. Within the same firm and fiscal year, the mix of activities in earnings calls and in statutory filings (10-K and 10-Q) is statistically indistinguishable. The share of activities with a quantified outcome, a named product or process, or a named provider is significantly lower in the filings. The design compares venue-level composition, not individual claims followed from call to filing. It shows that filings carry less evidence, not that specific call claims were withdrawn.

## Promotion is not the opposite of evidence

A common assumption in corporate communication research is that promotional tone and credibility move in opposite directions: heavy promotion means empty hype, and a sober tone means real operational grounding.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_words_gap = json.loads(_p("channel_gap_words_robustness.json").read_text())
promo_ratio = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
promo_call = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["call_mean"]
promo_filing = _words_gap["promo_per_1k_words"]["filing_mean"]
quant_ratio = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
quant_call = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["call_mean"]
quant_filing = _words_gap["quant_per_1k_words"]["filing_mean"]
```

The cross-venue data reject this trade-off. Per 1,000 words, earnings calls contain `{python} f"{promo_ratio:.1f}"`× more promotional statements than statutory filings (from `{python} f"{promo_filing:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{promo_call:.3f}"` claims per 1,000 words). They amplify quantification even more. Calls contain `{python} f"{quant_ratio:.1f}"`× more quantified outcome claims than filings (from `{python} f"{quant_filing:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{quant_call:.3f}"` claims per 1,000 words, @fig-promotion-and-evidence).


Promotion and evidence rise together across venues; they do not trade off. Filings sound unpromotional because their language is generic legal boilerplate, not because they are better grounded. Tone alone is not a proxy for credibility.

## Regulatory scrutiny as an external stress test

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
def _pp(rel):
    p = Path(f"../{rel}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(rel)
sec_cases = json.loads(_pp("data/processed/sec_comment_letter_cases.json").read_text())
sec_n_matched = sum(1 for d in sec_cases["letters"] if d["relevance"] != "outside universe")
sec_n_direct = sec_cases["relevance_counts"].get("direct", 0)
sec_n_adjacent = sec_cases["relevance_counts"].get("adjacent", 0)
_w = sec_cases["cases"]["WELL"]
_wk = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(_w["k"])}
def _wv(m, k, who="treated"):
    v = _w[who][m][_wk[k]] if k in _wk else None
    return "n/a" if v is None else f"{v:.3f}"
def _wd(m, who="treated"):
    a, b = _w[who][m][_wk[-1]], _w[who][m][_wk[0]]
    return "n/a" if a is None or b is None else f"{b - a:+.3f}"
_a = sec_cases["cases"]["ANET"]
_ak = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(_a["k"])}
def _ad(m, who="treated"):
    a, b = _a[who][m][_ak[-1]], _a[who][m][_ak[0]]
    return "n/a" if a is None or b is None else f"{b - a:+.3f}"
```

When the regulator questions a firm's AI claims directly, does the issuer fix the specific gap, and does it change its broader disclosure posture? The first finding is about how rare this is. We ran a full-text search of every SEC staff comment letter and company response filed from 2022 to 2026 for AI-related terms. We restricted it to the analysis universe and read each staff letter. The search matches the correspondence of `{python} sec_n_matched` issuers, but only `{python} sec_n_direct` letter questions a firm's own AI claims.

That letter is the Welltower letter of 2025-04-28. It contrasts a single 10-K sentence with the "industry-leading" platform claimed on the earnings call. It then asks the company to describe its data science platform and the status of its AI integration. One further letter is adjacent: Arista Networks was required to disclose revenue by customer sector, including "Cloud and AI Titans". The rest match AI terms for unrelated reasons: a segment named "HPC & AI", a climate-risk review, an activist's proxy materials. The full inventory, with what each letter actually asks, is in Appendix F (@tbl-g1-sec-letters).

Direct regulatory scrutiny of AI claims among the largest U.S. issuers is therefore not rare but singular, and that is itself informative. Through mid-2026 the SEC's stated concern with "AI washing" had produced one comment letter on AI claims to a firm in the S&P 500 of 2021.

Panel A: AI claim density; Panel B: realized-integration claims, the dimension the staff asked about. Descriptive comparison; no inference is drawn from a single treated firm."

The one direct case shows more AI text, not more grounded AI text (@fig-sec-welltower; full measures for both cases in @tbl-g2-sec-cases, Appendix F). In the first annual report filed after the letter, Welltower's AI claim density rose from `{python} _wv("claim_density", -1)` to `{python} _wv("claim_density", 0)` claims per thousand words (`{python} _wd("claim_density")`). That is the same size of rise as its matched peers' (`{python} _wd("claim_density", "controls_mean")`), so the firm added AI text at the industry's pace. The dimension the staff asked about, realized integration, moved from `{python} _wv("realized_density", -1)` to `{python} _wv("realized_density", 0)` (`{python} _wd("realized_density")`), less than at peers (`{python} _wd("realized_density", "controls_mean")`). A first quantified metric appeared (`{python} _wv("quant_density", 0)` per thousand words). Decoupling moved from `{python} _wv("w", -1)` to `{python} _wv("w", 0)`: the firm's disclosure rank rose faster than its substance rank.

The adjacent Arista case has the same shape. Claim density rose by `{python} _ad("claim_density")` after the segment-reporting letters against `{python} _ad("claim_density", "controls_mean")` at peers, with no change in quantified-metric density (`{python} _ad("quant_density")`).

Two cases cannot test H3's regulatory clause; they are consistent with it. Where substantiation was requested, the observable response was more AI text rather than measurably more grounded AI text. The cheap-talk account of scrutiny survives the only direct test the data allow.

## What credibility means in this thesis

Three things survive the climb up the ladder. Decoupling between narrative intensity and grounded substance is persistent (year-over-year $\rho =$ `{python} f"{hd_w_rho:.2f}"`). The cross-venue gap comes from missing evidence in statutory filings, not from a different mix of activities. And direct regulatory scrutiny of AI claims is so rare among large issuers that it amounts to a single case. In that case the response was more AI text rather than a narrower gap between talk and grounded activity. AI washing in this thesis therefore means an observable, persistent Decoupling ($W$) between narrative intensity and grounded operational substance, not legal proof of fraud or nonimplementation.

# Market Relevance of Disclosure Signals

Does the systematic risk the market assigns to a firm after an earnings call follow the *volume* of its AI talk or the *substance* of its disclosed activity? The outcome throughout is post-call market beta conditioned on pre-call beta. We ask whether AI disclosure carries information about how the market prices a firm's risk, not whether it earns abnormal returns. We track communication call by call across S&P 500 firms from 2021 to 2025, separating a firm's established disclosure posture from the surprise content of a given call.

## Empirical strategy and research design

The unit of observation is a firm-date earnings call event. Transcripts from the same day are aggregated, and calls with zero AI mentions stay in the sample as valid zeros. The call date anchors the timeline:

- **Historical Posture ($\text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}}, \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}}$):** Expanding mean of disclosure intensity and substance across calls strictly prior to date $t$.
- **Call-Specific Surprise ($\text{SurpriseD}_{i,t}, \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t}$):** Current call value minus the firm's historical mean ($\text{Value}_{i,t} - \text{Hist}_{i,t^{-}}$).
- **Disclosure Intensity ($D$):** AI frames per 1,000 words.
- **Disclosed Substance ($S$):** $S = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities}}) \times G$, where activity grounding ($G$) is the proportion of activities meeting concrete verification criteria.

Pre- and post-call market betas are estimated over non-overlapping windows to avoid look-ahead bias and earnings-announcement drift:

- $\beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$ over $[-252, -21]$ trading days before the call.
- $\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t}$ over $[+21, +126]$ trading days after the call.

Predetermined controls ($X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$) are log market cap, 60-day return momentum ($\text{Return}_{60}$), and pre-call idiosyncratic volatility. Point-in-time accounting fundamentals (ROA, leverage) come from the most recent 10-K or 10-Q filed strictly before the call ($\text{filing\_date} < \text{call\_date}$), extracted from XBRL accession facts.

## Baseline econometric model

We estimate an ANCOVA specification conditioning on pre-call beta:

$$
\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_2 \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_3 \text{SurpriseD}_{i,t} + \beta_4 \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t} + \gamma \beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \delta X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \alpha_{s,y} + \epsilon_{i,t},
$$

with industry-by-year fixed effects ($\alpha_{s,y} \equiv \text{SIC2} \times \text{Year}$) and standard errors clustered by firm. Continuous regressors are standardized to zero mean and unit variance.

@tbl-call-beta-baseline and @fig-call-beta-baseline report the baseline estimates.

The baseline covers `{python} f"{int(_formal['n_calls']):,}"` calls across `{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_firms'])` firms (`{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_fe_cells'])` industry-by-year cells). The median firm has `{python} f"{_baseline_sample['median_prior_calls']:.1f}"` prior calls in the panel, so the historical averages rest on a solid base. The same sample and specification underlie every robustness column in @tbl-call-beta-paper. The accounting-control specification, which needs quarterly balance-sheet data, is estimated on the subsample where those data exist and is reported with its own sample size.

Two patterns stand out:

1. **Disclosure is `{python} _sig(sd_p)` at the call-specific margin:** Historical disclosure intensity is `{python} _sig(hd_p)` ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hd_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hd_pstr`); call-specific surprise disclosure is $\beta =$ `{python} f"{sd_b:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} sd_pstr`). An established disclosure posture is robustly associated with subsequent systematic risk conditional on pre-call beta; the disclosure surprise of a single call is not.
2. **Substance does not:** Historical substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hs_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hs_pstr`) and surprise substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{ss_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} ss_pstr`) are indistinguishable from zero. Joint tests say the same: the disclosure block ($\text{HistD} + \text{SurpriseD}$) is significant ($F =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['p']:.3f}"`; partial $R^2 =$ `{python} f"{_partial_r2:.4f}"`), while the substance block is null ($F =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['p']:.3f}"`).

## Incremental information of decoupling

Decoupling ($W$) adds nothing to the beta model once its two components are already in it. Adding firm-year $W$ to the specification estimated on the `{python} f"{hd_inc_n:,}"` firm-year observations with a matched prior-year $W$ raises $R^2$ from `{python} f"{hd_inc_r2_base:.4f}"` to `{python} f"{hd_inc_r2_w:.4f}"` ($\Delta R^2 =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_dr2:+.4f}"`; Wald $F =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_F:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_p:.3f}"`). Decoupling remains a persistent and managerially useful diligence signal, but in this specification it carries no incremental information about systematic risk once Disclosure Intensity and Disclosed Substance are in the model. On this evidence the market responds to the level of AI talk, not to disclosed substance and not to the gap between the two.

The baseline result survives accounting controls (ROA and liabilities/assets), longer post-call horizons (up to a full trading year, $[+21, +252]$), and the Fama–French three-factor benchmark. It weakens and disappears, however, under within-firm (firm fixed effects) and first-difference ($\Delta\beta$) specifications. The association is therefore mostly cross-sectional sorting, not a call-induced change in systematic risk. Firms that talk heavily about AI carry higher market risk than peers, but quarter-to-quarter shifts in disclosure are not associated with within-firm changes in beta. Full diagnostics, leverage specifications (Debt/Equity and Liabilities/Assets), and influence tests are in Appendix E.

```{python}
_pb_disc_p = "< 0.001" if pb_disc["p"] < 0.001 else f"= {pb_disc['p']:.3f}"
```

## Interpretation and limits

1. **HistDisclosure is not concentrated in a single year, but SurpriseDisclosure never reaches significance on its own:** Leave-one-year-out regressions keep $\text{HistDisclosure}$ `{python} _hd_sig_text` ($p \le$ `{python} f"{_max_p_hd:.3f}" + _hd_detail_text`). $\text{SurpriseDisclosure}$, by contrast, `{python} "reaches p < 0.05 in at least one excluded-year specification" if _any_sd_sig else "never reaches conventional significance in any single-year exclusion"`, consistent with its null in the baseline. The association between call disclosure and post-call beta runs through a firm's persistent historical posture, not through the surprise content of any one call.
2. **Pre-call beta placebo failure:** Regressing pre-call beta ($\beta^{\text{pre}}_{[-252, -21]}$) on contemporaneous call disclosure yields $\beta =$ `{python} f"{pb_disc['beta_std']:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} _pb_disc_p`), while substance is null ($p$ `{python} _pb_sub_p`). Firms that talk heavily about AI were already high-beta before the call, which is the cross-sectional reading of the robustness table.

# From Measurement to Managerial Application

The pipeline built and tested on `{python} hd_paragraphs_m` million paragraphs of corporate text boils down to six diagnostic questions. Five follow the measurement chain ($D \to A \to G \to S \to W$). The sixth asks whether a firm tells the same story in its calls and in its filings. @tbl-managerial-framework reads each one as a managerial and investment decision.

| Core Due-Diligence Question | Construct | Managerial & Investment Decision Read |
|---|---|---|
| **1. How much are they saying?** | Disclosure Intensity ($D$) | **Narrative Exposure:** Evaluates corporate attention to AI. High $D$ signals ambition or growth positioning, but absent grounding carries high rhetorical risk. |
| **2. What do they claim to be doing?** | Disclosed AI Activity ($A$) | **Claimed Scope:** Records whether the firm reports actionable initiatives across core business functions rather than relying on abstract buzzwords. |
| **3. How concrete is the disclosure?** | AI Activity Grounding ($G$) | **Evidentiary Rigor:** Assesses grounding attributes (scaled deployment, named product/process, quantified metric, provider transparency). |
| **4. How much grounded substance is disclosed?** | Disclosed Substance ($S$) | **Effective Substantiation:** Evaluates total volume of grounded AI activity, rewarding operational depth while penalizing empty boilerplate. |
| **5. Is narrative running ahead of execution?** | Decoupling ($W$) | **Triage / Diligence Signal:** Flags firms whose narrative volume outstrips grounded operational disclosure ($W \gg 0$) or quiet executors ($W \ll 0$). |
| **6. Does the story survive across venues?** | Cross-Venue Consistency | **Evidentiary Commitment:** Checks whether oral conference-call claims, metrics, and products are formally committed to statutory 10-Ks under legal liability. |

: The AI Disclosure Credibility Framework: translating measurement constructs into managerial decisions. {#tbl-managerial-framework}

## Applying the framework: worked corporate examples

We now run the framework on contrasting firm-years from the S&P 500 (@tbl-firm-comparisons). Corporate AI communication changes fast from one reporting cycle to the next, so we look at specific firm-years rather than multi-year averages. That is where disclosure intensity, grounding and cross-venue divergence show up in real filings and real regulatory review.

```{python}
_ws["pct_s"] = _ws.groupby("year")["substance"].rank(pct=True) * 100
_dim = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet")).set_index("ticker")["archetype"]

    UNION ALL SELECT accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us'
""").df()
con.close()

    return f"{p}{suf}"

for t, name, y in CASES:

        rows["prop"].append(f"{(a['ai_source'] == 'own').mean() * 100:.1f}% proprietary")
    else:

static = {
    "posture": ["Governance, internal deployment", "Legal caution, risk avoidance", "Promotional + high specificity", "Privacy, ethical governance", "Cross-venue divergence (promotional call vs. risk boilerplate in 10-K)"],
    "claim": ['*"Models and estimations that JPMorgan Chase uses, including those incorporating machine learning, are periodically reviewed and modified under firmwide governance."* (10-K)',
              '*"The emergence and adoption of new technologies, including AI, require us to invest resources to adapt... and present operational and competitive risks."* (10-K Item 1A)',
              '*"Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 68% driven by scaling AI infrastructure and usage, offset by efficiency gains in Azure."* (10-Q)',
              '*"Apple has been and will continue to be deliberate and thoughtful in deployment... guided by our privacy principles and on-device processing."* (DEF 14A)',
              '**10-K (p. 40):** *"Integrating generative AI tools into our systems"* vs. **Q4 Call:** *"Industry-leading data science platform [as a] competitive advantage"* → **SEC Inquiry:** *"Tell us, and revise future filings, to discuss your platform and status of AI integration."*'],
    "notice": ["High governance discipline masked by moderate disclosure volume; internal workflow integration prioritized over commercial hype.",
               "Risk-factor-dominated disclosure: high legal-risk orientation, low grounding, and few deployed AI activities disclosed in the 10-K; the filing tells a reader what could go wrong, not what the firm is doing.",
               "Exceptional promotional intensity backed by deep disclosed operational substance and quantified commercial traction.",
               "Disciplined narrative volume prioritizing on-device privacy governance and brand protection over speculative monetization.",
               "**The archetypal regulatory trigger:** sharp cross-venue asymmetry where oral claims on earnings calls outpaced statutory 10-K filings, drawing a formal SEC comment letter."],
}
table = [
    ["**Disclosure Archetype**"] + rows["arch"],
    ["**Dominant Posture**"] + static["posture"],
    ["**Disclosure Intensity ($D$)**"] + rows["D"],
    ["**Disclosed AI Activities ($A$)**"] + rows["A"],
    ["**AI Activity Grounding ($G$)**"] + rows["G"],
    ["**Disclosed Substance ($S$)**"] + rows["S"],
    ["**Decoupling ($W$)**"] + rows["W"],
    ["**Deployed / Scaled Share**"] + rows["dep"],
    ["**Internal vs. Customer Focus**"] + rows["focus"],
    ["**Proprietary Tech Share**"] + rows["prop"],
    ["**Representative AI Claim / Venue Contrast**"] + static["claim"],
    ["**What Investors & Regulators Should Notice**"] + static["notice"],
]
Markdown(tabulate(table, headers=["Feature / Dimension"] + cols))
```

**Microsoft (MSFT):** Microsoft shows that loud communication is not the same as decoupling. Its disclosure volume is exceptional ($D =$ `{python} f"{cv['MSFT']['frames_per_1k']:.3f}"`, `{python} _ord(cv['MSFT']['pct_d'])` percentile). But it is backed by one of the deepest AI activity inventories in the corpus ($A =$ `{python} int(cv['MSFT']['n_activities'])` in the 2024 filing year) and strong operational grounding ($S =$ `{python} f"{cv['MSFT']['substance']:.3f}"`). The talk and the substance match ($W =$ `{python} f"{cv['MSFT']['w']:+.3f}"`).

**JPMorgan Chase (JPM) vs. Goldman Sachs (GS):** Two banks with similar disclosure intensity can look very different underneath. In the 2024 filing year both report moderate intensity ($D =$ `{python} f"{cv['JPM']['frames_per_1k']:.3f}"` and `{python} f"{cv['GS']['frames_per_1k']:.3f}"`). JPM anchors its communication in formal governance oversight ($G =$ `{python} f"{cv['JPM']['grounding_index']:.3f}"`) and internal workflow integration. Goldman's AI disclosures sit mostly in defensive legal risk factors. Its grounding is lower and its gap between talk and disclosed substance wider ($G =$ `{python} f"{cv['GS']['grounding_index']:.3f}"`, $W =$ `{python} f"{cv['GS']['w']:+.3f}"` versus `{python} f"{cv['JPM']['w']:+.3f}"` for JPM).

**Apple (AAPL):** Apple is the Governance-Led posture in practice. Its communication stresses proprietary on-device processing and consumer privacy rather than speculative commercial claims, and it keeps narrative volume in line with its operational footprint ($D =$ `{python} f"{cv['AAPL']['frames_per_1k']:.3f}"`, $W =$ `{python} f"{cv['AAPL']['w']:+.3f}"`).

**Welltower (WELL, SEC comment letter):** Welltower is the case where cross-venue divergence met a regulator. In its Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, its AI disclosure was a single generic statement on page 40. The firm was "integrating generative AI tools into [its] systems" ($D =$ `{python} f"{cv['WELL']['frames_per_1k']:.3f}" if 'WELL' in cv else "n/a"` in the 2025 filing year). On its fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call (February 12, 2025), executives described an "industry-leading" proprietary data science platform as a primary competitive advantage. On April 28, 2025, the SEC Division of Corporation Finance issued a formal comment letter citing this gap between venues. It asked management to explain the gap and to disclose the platform's actual operational status in statutory filings [@welltower2025letter, p. 1].

## Portfolio-scale application: screening the S&P 500

### The AI disclosure decision heuristic for due diligence

The framework does not sort firms into fixed classes. It organizes due diligence with a 2×2 heuristic built on Disclosure Intensity ($D$) and Disclosed Substance ($S$) (@tbl-screening-matrix). $W$ is not a fraud classifier ($W \neq \text{Legal Wrongdoing}$): $D$ and $S$ decide the action for each quadrant, and $W$ decides how deep to dig inside it. Quadrants come from a median split of $D$ and of $S$ among the firms disclosing AI in the FY2026 cycle. By construction the two high-$D$ cells and the two high-$S$ cells each hold half of the disclosers; what matters is how the two splits cross.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

_wall = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))
_m26 = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_master_v2.parquet"))
_m26 = _m26[_m26["year"] == 2026]
scr_n_index = int(_m26["ticker"].nunique())
_d26 = _wall[(_wall["year"] == 2026) & (_wall["any_ai"] == 1.0)].drop_duplicates("ticker")
scr_n_disc = len(_d26)
scr_n_nondisc = scr_n_index - scr_n_disc
_hiD = _d26["frames_per_1k"] >= _d26["frames_per_1k"].median()
_hiS = _d26["substance"] >= _d26["substance"].median()
scr = {
    "investigate": int((_hiD & ~_hiS).sum()),
    "validate": int((_hiD & _hiS).sum()),
    "explore": int((~_hiD & _hiS).sum()),
    "deprior": int((~_hiD & ~_hiS).sum()),
}
scr_pct = {k: v / scr_n_disc * 100 for k, v in scr.items()}
scr_deprior_total = scr["deprior"] + scr_n_nondisc
scr_deprior_total_pct = scr_deprior_total / scr_n_index * 100
_q95 = _wall.loc[_wall["any_ai"] == 1.0, "w"].quantile(0.95)
scr_tail = int((_d26["w"] >= _q95).sum())
scr_neg = int((_d26["w"] < 0).sum())
_g = pd.read_parquet(_p("channel_gap_cells.parquet"))
_g26 = _g[_g["t"].astype(str) == "2026"]
_zgap = (_g26["gap_promo_per_1k"] - _g26["gap_promo_per_1k"].mean()) / _g26["gap_promo_per_1k"].std()
scr_n_dual = len(_g26)
scr_n_gap = int((_zgap > 1.5).sum())
```

| | Low Disclosed Substance ($S$) | High Disclosed Substance ($S$) |
|---|---|---|
| **High Disclosure Intensity ($D$)** | **INVESTIGATE** (`{python} scr["investigate"]` firms, `{python} f"{scr_pct['investigate']:.1f}"`%)<br>Audit claims, examine operational stage, metrics, products, and providers; compare oral calls against statutory filings ($W \gg 0$). | **VALIDATE** (`{python} scr["validate"]` firms, `{python} f"{scr_pct['validate']:.1f}"`%)<br>Confirm documented evidence is cross-venue consistent and grounding is sustained over reporting periods ($W \approx 0$). |
| **Low Disclosure Intensity ($D$)** | **DEPRIORITIZE / MONITOR** (`{python} scr_deprior_total` firms incl. non-disclosers, `{python} f"{scr_deprior_total_pct:.1f}"`% of index)<br>Low narrative exposure with minimal reported activity; requires no active diligence unless corporate posture shifts ($W \approx 0$). | **EXPLORE** (`{python} scr["explore"]` firms, `{python} f"{scr_pct['explore']:.1f}"`%)<br>Investigate quiet substance: concrete, grounded operational capability deployed under minimal promotional fanfare ($W \ll 0$). |

: AI Disclosure Decision Heuristic: turning disclosure intensity and disclosed substance into due-diligence action, showing the empirical distribution of S&P 500 issuers in the 2026 reporting season (`{python} scr_n_index` firms with a 2026 filing; `{python} scr_n_disc` disclosing issuers evaluated year-to-date; percentages in the three disclosing cells are shares of disclosers). *Disclosure Intensity ($D$) and Disclosed Substance ($S$) are the empirical measures defined in the methodology; the heuristic organizes action priorities without introducing additional corporate typologies.* {#tbl-screening-matrix}

### Four operational portfolio screens

Two further cuts sharpen the quadrant counts in @tbl-screening-matrix. Inside the Investigate cell, `{python} scr_tail` FY2026 firm-years sit above the 95th percentile of $W$ in the full 2021–2026 panel. And `{python} scr_neg` disclosers have negative $W$ (substance rank above disclosure rank), the pool the Explore cell draws from. A fifth screen, Reconcile, cuts across the quadrants. It starts from the `{python} scr_n_dual` issuers with both a 2026 call and a 2026 filing. Of these, `{python} scr_n_gap` show a call-minus-filing promotional gap more than 1.5 standard deviations above the 2026 mean ($Z_{\text{gap}} > 1.5$), the Welltower pattern.

@tbl-screening-screens runs the screens on representative FY2026 issuers, evaluated year to date. The named firms are the three highest and lowest values of $W$ and the three highest values of $S$ among 2026 disclosers, plus the two firms with the largest cross-venue promotional gap. The labels say where each firm falls in the distribution of its own disclosures; they say nothing about whether those disclosures are accurate.
